These stages are approximate, as menstrual cycles and hormonal patterns vary from person to person.
A consistent skincare routine can help reduce recurring breakouts. Some useful practices include:
If breakouts occur around the same time every month, start paying attention to your skin before your expected period.
Getting seven to eight hours of sleep, managing stress, and maintaining a balanced diet can support overall skin health. Limiting excessive sugary and highly processed foods may also help some people manage acne.
Keeping a diary of your menstrual cycle and breakouts for two to three months can help identify recurring patterns.
If acne becomes painful, persists, or leaves scars, consult a dermatologist for appropriate treatment.

item.title: Sleeping for eight hours but still waking up exhausted?
item.description:
Even after a full night's sleep, waking up feeling exhausted or sluggish is not uncommon. However, if morning fatigue becomes a regular occurrence, it may be worth taking a closer look at your daily routine. Certain everyday habits can affect sleep quality, energy levels, and overall well-being. Making a few simple changes may help you feel more refreshed throughout the day.
Spending long hours watching reels, scrolling through social media, or playing games in bed is a common habit. However, excessive screen time before bedtime can interfere with sleep. The bright light from mobile screens can keep the brain alert and make it harder to fall asleep. As a result, even after getting eight hours of sleep, poor sleep quality may leave you feeling tired the following morning.
Skipping breakfast or regularly delaying meals can affect blood sugar levels, potentially leading to fatigue and headaches. Sugary foods or light snacks may provide a temporary energy boost, but the effect often wears off quickly, leaving you feeling sluggish. In contrast, balanced meals containing adequate protein can help maintain steady energy levels throughout the day.
Insufficient water intake can lead to dehydration, which may cause sluggishness, drowsiness, and difficulty concentrating. People who spend long hours working in air-conditioned rooms may also forget to drink enough water throughout the day. Along with plain water, drinks such as lemon water, coconut water, and buttermilk can help replenish fluids and maintain hydration.
Spending most of the day sitting at a desk can also contribute to fatigue. Remaining physically inactive for extended periods may affect blood circulation and cause muscle stiffness. Taking short breaks to stand up, stretch, or walk around can help keep the body active. A brief movement break every hour can make a difference in how you feel throughout the day.
Tea and coffee may provide a temporary energy boost, but excessive caffeine consumption can interfere with sleep. Drinking caffeinated beverages, particularly in the afternoon or evening, may make it difficult to fall asleep at night. Poor sleep can then contribute to tiredness the following morning. Switching to caffeine-free herbal tea, especially later in the day, may be a better alternative.
If morning fatigue continues for weeks despite making changes to your daily habits, it is important to consult a doctor. Persistent tiredness may sometimes be linked to underlying health conditions, including iron, vitamin D, or vitamin B12 deficiencies, as well as thyroid disorders. Identifying the underlying cause can help ensure appropriate treatment and improve overall well-being.

item.title: OBHIZATRIK Foundation holds meeting for ‘Breathing Dhaka’ project on air quality monitoring
item.description:
OBHIZATRIK Foundation has launched an initiative to expand air pollution monitoring across Dhaka, particularly in underserved communities, through a network of hyperlocal PM2.5 monitoring devices.
The foundation held an inception meeting of its project titled “Breathing Dhaka: Open-Access Hyperlocal PM2.5 Monitoring in Underserved Communities” at the Department of Environment (DoE) headquarters in Agargaon on Tuesday.
The project is supported by the Air Quality Fund 2026 of the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC).
DoE Director General Md Lutfor Rahman attended the meeting as chief guest, while OBHIZATRIK Foundation president Ahmed Imtiaz Jami presented the project's objectives and implementation plan.
Ahmad Kamruzzaman Majumder, chairman of the Center for Atmospheric Pollution Studies and technical lead of the project, outlined its technical aspects.
Speaking at the meeting, Lutfor Rahman said the initiative would play an important role in monitoring Dhaka's air quality and expressed hope that such efforts would help the capital move out of the list of the world's most polluted cities.
Jami said the foundation works with underprivileged communities, which are among the most vulnerable to the harmful effects of air pollution.
Through the initiative, the foundation aims to monitor air quality, work with government and non-government stakeholders, contribute to policy development and raise public awareness through social and behavioural change programs, he said.
Majumder said air quality monitoring devices would be installed in eight low-income, industrial-adjacent and pollution-vulnerable areas across Dhaka.
The devices will collect data continuously for 12 months, with the findings regularly cross-validated against data from the Department of Environment, he said.
The collected data will be made publicly accessible, while research papers will also be published based on the findings, he added.
The project aims to establish a monitoring network covering different parts of Dhaka, with particular focus on communities that have long remained underserved in air quality monitoring.
The inception meeting discussed the implementation strategy, installation of PM2.5 sensors and selection of potential monitoring locations. Participants also shared recommendations on the project's implementation and future activities.
Among those attending were Farid Ahmed, director of the DoE's Dhaka Metropolitan Office; Mohammad Abdul Motalib and Begum Shahnaj Rahman, deputy directors of its Air Quality Management Division; Tanjina Akter, assistant director of the division; Tapan Kumar Nath, deputy secretary; Ruhul Amin, assistant project director of BRCP-1 and assistant engineer of the Bangladesh Land Port Authority; and Dr Mohammad Safiur Rahman, chief scientific officer and head of division at the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Commission.
Officials from government and non-government development organizations, along with faculty members from Stamford University Bangladesh and Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (Buet), also attended the meeting.
The initiative is expected to generate community-level air quality data to support environmental research, pollution monitoring and evidence-based policymaking.

item.title: Imagine Sisyphus happy: Why Albert Camus still matters
item.description:
There is something almost comical about being human. We wake up, go to work, earn money, pay bills, worry about the future, and go to sleep, only to repeat everything the following morning. We call it life. But occasionally, when we are too exhausted to distract ourselves, an uncomfortable question emerges: What is the point of all this?
Born on 7 November 1913, the French-Algerian writer and philosopher Albert Camus spent his life confronting the absurdity of human existence.
More than six decades after his death, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) and The Outsider (1942) speak to a world struggling with suffering, contradictions, and uncertainty.
In 2026, Camus is not merely relevant. He is necessary.
The absurdity of being alive
In The Myth of Sisyphus , Camus identifies suicide as philosophy's most serious problem. Before debating justice, morality or religion, we must confront a fundamental question: Is life worth living?
Camus calls the confrontation between our hunger for meaning and the universe's silence the absurd.
We want justice, but injustice persists.
We want permanence, but everything changes.
We want suffering to mean something, yet the world offers no guaranteed explanation.
Consider an ordinary Bangladeshi citizen struggling through traffic, working long hours, and worrying about rising living costs or a graduate who studies for years only to discover that education does not guarantee employment.
We are told to work harder and remain patient, even when circumstances make those promises seem hollow.
Camus offers neither blind optimism nor surrender. He proposes revolt: the conscious decision to live and struggle without pretending that the universe owes us answers.
We need not discover an ultimate meaning before we can begin living meaningfully.
Meursault and the society that puts us on trial
If The Myth of Sisyphus articulates the philosophical problem, The Outsider gives it a human face. Meursault (protagonist of The Outsider ) refuses to perform the grief expected of him at his mother's funeral. Later, after killing an Arab man on a beach, he faces a trial in which his emotional indifference becomes almost as important as the crime itself.
Society seems disturbed not only by what he has done but also by his refusal to behave like a conventional son.
Meursault is no uncomplicated hero. He commits a killing, and his indifference raises serious moral questions.
Moreover, the unnamed Arab victim exposes a troubling colonial silence: the European protagonist receives an elaborate interior life, while the man he kills remains largely without a name or voice. Reading Camus critically means acknowledging this imbalance.
Nevertheless, Meursault forces us to ask: Do we judge people for their actions, or also punish them for refusing to perform the emotions we expect?
In Bangladesh, where family honor, religious conventions, social reputation and communal expectations shape individual lives, this question remains urgent.
Social media intensifies the problem: a photograph, an unfortunate sentence or an unconventional response can become grounds for public condemnation. We demand authenticity but punish those who refuse our preferred scripts.
Meursault's trial challenges us to distinguish genuine wrongdoing from discomfort with difference.
How much of what we call morality is morality, and how much is simply obedience to social expectations?
Why Camus matters in 2026
Our world is saturated with explanations but strangely impoverished in understanding. Political ideologies promise perfect futures, digital platforms reward outrage, and advertising teaches us to measure ourselves against manufactured images of happiness. Certainty often matters more than truth.
Camus distrusts the temptation to justify present suffering in the name of an imagined perfect future. For Bangladesh, this is no abstract concern. Amid economic pressures, questions of justice and accountability, environmental vulnerability and competing promises of development, we are frequently asked to endure today's difficulties for tomorrow's rewards. Sometimes endurance is necessary. But when does patience become an excuse for injustice? When does hope become a substitute for action?
Camus does not ask us to abandon collective struggle. If no cosmic script guarantees justice, our responsibility to build just institutions and protect one another becomes more urgent, not less. His philosophy also speaks to our digital age: we can remain permanently connected through screens while feeling profoundly isolated. Acknowledging life's difficulties may be more liberating than pretending everything is fine. We need neither absolute certainty to oppose injustice nor manufactured optimism to care for others.
One must imagine Sisyphus happy
In Greek mythology, Sisyphus is condemned to push a boulder uphill, only to watch it roll back down. He must begin again, endlessly. Camus recognizes our condition in this punishment: we struggle, lose, rebuild and begin again, often without knowing whether our efforts will ultimately succeed.
Yet The Myth of Sisyphus concludes: “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”
Not because suffering is pleasant, but because Sisyphus confronts his condition without surrendering to it. His revolt lies in continuing without illusion. Perhaps we are all pushing something uphill: a degree, a career, a family, a country, a fragile hope that tomorrow might be less difficult. But we must not romanticize poverty or tell the exhausted simply to be happy. Happiness cannot replace fair wages, social justice or the conditions necessary for a dignified life. Accepting reality must never mean refusing to change it.
And what about Meursault?
If Sisyphus teaches us to confront our condition, Meursault exposes the social rituals through which we disguise it. Yet his moral failures remind us that personal freedom cannot mean indifference to others. Perhaps we are all Sisyphus and Meursault in different proportions: exhausted by repetition, alienated by expectations, tempted by indifference, and still searching for a way to live honestly.
We should therefore resist turning Camus into another inspirational quotation on a social media post. His philosophy offers no magical escape from the absurd. It offers something more difficult and more useful: the courage to see clearly, to resist what diminishes human dignity, to care without guarantees, and to continue living without lying to ourselves.
The boulder will roll back. The world will remain imperfect. Our questions may never receive final answers. But we can still decide how we meet the mountain, what we do for those climbing beside us, and whether we allow the absurdity of existence to make us cruel or more compassionate.
Perhaps that is what it means to imagine Sisyphus happy: not to pretend that life is easy, but to refuse to let its difficulty have the final word.
Kallol Bain is a lecturer in the Department of English at Daffodil International University.

item.title: ‘Ugliness cannot be airbrushed out of art’
item.description:
Kaiser Haq has never tried to make Dhaka prettier than it is. Born in the city, the poet, essayist, and translator has been writing poems about it since the 1960s, full of its noise, crowds, and smells.
His first two collections, Starting Lines and A Little Ado , appeared in 1978. They were followed by A Happy Farewell (1994), Black Orchid (1996), The Logopathic Reviewer’s Song (2002), and Pariah and Other Poems .
The enlarged edition of Published in the Streets of Dhaka adds new poems, among them “Ode on the Lungi,” which takes an everyday garment as its subject. He has also parodied Jibanananda’s “ Banalata Sen ,” setting it in the city.
He translated the Selected Poems of Shamsur Rahman (1985) and Rabindranath Tagore’s novel Chaturanga , published in English as Quartet (1993). He also retold the legend of the goddess Manasa in The Triumph of the Snake Goddess , published by Harvard University Press.
In this conversation with Arts and Letters, Kaiser Haq talks about why ugliness belongs in poetry, what Dhaka has lost, and writing in English.
AnL: Your poems have been set in Dhaka for decades. Is there a version of the city you can no longer see, because you have written it so many times that it has become more of a poem than a place?
Kaiser Haq: I don’t think so, because Dhaka is constantly changing. The salient aspects of my poetic take on the cityscape and its people haven’t changed, but I can see new pressures on the infrastructure and the inhabitants. I am trying to figure out how to make poetry out of this ever-changing Dhaka.
Your poems keep the noise, the crowds, and the smells of Dhaka. Why does ugliness matter to you as material, and what does prettifying the city cost a poem?
The ugliness of the city cannot be airbrushed out of art and literature without slipping into escapism. Besides, I think I’m enough of a Baudelairian to take the ugliness as legitimate material for poetry.
Has the city lost something in your lifetime that you quietly mourn?
Dhaka is a small town that has grown into a conurbation, the second largest in the world in terms of population, without acquiring the civic infrastructure that gives city life its distinctive feel. The Dhaka I feel most at home in no longer exists. It is the Dhaka of my childhood and boyhood years, when there was a sense of community and a lively literary scene. Daily adda brought together poets, fiction writers, artists, and filmmakers.
You rework a Bengali classic, setting it in modern Dhaka. What did you want to keep from it, and what did you change?
You are referring to my parody of “Banalata Sen,” right? I love Jibanananda’s poetry. In that parody, I think I have captured the essence of that particular poem within the parameters of Dhaka’s urban ambience. Of course, in the process, I have added a spritz of humor.
Photo: Abir Ahmmed Shupto/Dhaka Tribune
Your poetic persona has been described as that of a flâneur wandering through Dhaka, though you were born into the city. Does the label fit what you do?
Flâneurs belong to the cities they wander in. You don’t wander into it; you stroll around it, observing life in its myriad forms. Sadly, the crush of overpopulation has destroyed the scope for flâneurie. The city needs a thorough overhaul, like the redesign of Paris by the city planner Baron Haussmann.
You say Dhaka’s ugliness cannot be airbrushed out of art, yet you want the city overhauled. Do those two positions pull against each other?
There is a difference between airbrushing something out of poetry and rebuilding a city. Baudelaire indulged in flâneurie as Haussmann was restructuring Paris. The poetic result was Les Fleurs du Mal. Haussmann’s work was commissioned to make the city more easily administered and controlled. Long, elegant boulevards and avenues would give a clear field of fire to soldiers facing rebels and mobs. That’s the sinister side of building a more beautiful Paris.
You write about a deeply Bengali city in the language of its former colonizers. Do you ever feel like a translator of Dhaka rather than a native son, as if the city must pass through English before it becomes yours on the page?
That’s a loaded question. I grew up in Dhaka, speaking Bangla at home and with my mohalla friends and English in my English-medium schools. I hope my use of English does not seem to be something imposed. I hope it has evolved into an acceptable vehicle for my observations and lucubrations. If you look at Kipling’s stories, you will see that the English language can effectively capture the tenor of Indian life. I try to achieve a similar effect.
Many postcolonial writers and readers keep their distance from Kipling. Why do you turn to him?
I’m aware of the postcolonial knee-jerk reaction to writers like Kipling. I reject it completely. Kipling was an imperialist, no doubt, but he was also Indian by birth, so to speak, and has given a vivid and realistic portrait of colonial India. As with all writing, we have to read him critically. But there is much a postcolonial writer can learn from him.
What are you working on next?
I’m thinking of a “New and Selected Poems.”
If Dhaka disappeared and only your poems survived, what would future readers make of the city?
Who can say? It depends on the upbringing and orientation of the people in the future. If they are aware of the peculiar aspects of South Asian city life in our time, whether from books or films and paintings and photographs, they will be able to relate to my poetry, just as we can relate to, say, Cavafy’s Alexandria.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,263 as 6 die in 24hrs
item.description:
Six more children died with measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours ending at 8am on Tuesday, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 1,263 this year.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) classified the latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.
With this, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,158, while confirmed deaths have remained the same at 105.
A total of 1,318 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, taking the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 232,823.
Meanwhile, 82 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, pushing laboratory-confirmed infections to 24,073.
Since March 15 this year, a total of 207,428 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country, of whom 198,752 have recovered, according to the DGHS.

item.title: HRFB expresses concern over sedition case against Satkhira rights activist
item.description:
Human Rights Forum Bangladesh (HRFB) has expressed deep concern over the filing of a sedition case against Shampa Goswami, executive director of Prerona Women Development Organisation in Satkhira, and fears that she may face further harassment and security risks.
According to information received from reliable sources, a case was filed against Shampa under Section 124A of the Bangladesh Penal Code at Shyamnagar police station in Satkhira on September 29, 2026.
Shampa has alleged that police surveillance is being conducted at her residence and her organisation’s office, while her family members are also being harassed.
In a statement, HRFB said allegations of this nature require particular consideration of the fundamental rights and privacy protections guaranteed by the Constitution of Bangladesh.
It noted that Article 36 of the Constitution guarantees citizens the right to freedom of movement, while Article 43 protects the privacy of the home and correspondence.
The organisation said allegations of surveillance at an individual's residence and workplace, as well as harassment of family members, must be treated with due seriousness.
HRFB also stressed that specific allegations are essential when bringing serious criminal charges, such as sedition, against individuals involved in human rights activities.
The forum called on the relevant authorities to examine the legal basis of the case against Shampa and verify the allegations, while also conducting an impartial investigation into the complaints she has raised.
It further urged the authorities to ensure that Shampa can continue her peaceful and legitimate human rights activities, including participating in international forums.
HRFB also called for appropriate measures to protect Shampa, her family members, and the staff and volunteers of the women's development organisation from intimidation, harassment or retaliatory action.
The statement was signed by Tahmina Rahman, convener of Human Rights Forum Bangladesh and executive director of Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK).

item.title: Workshop calls for evidence-based approach to tackling corruption
item.description:
A two-day national workshop on strengthening evidence-based approaches to measuring corruption and improving accountability in Bangladesh concluded at the Six Seasons Hotel in Gulshan-2, Dhaka, on Tuesday.
Titled “Measuring Corruption for Reform: Strengthening Evidence and Accountability in Bangladesh,” the workshop was jointly organised by the U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre, its partner embassies of Switzerland, Norway, the UK, Denmark and Germany, and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).
The workshop brought together government officials, development partners, academics, civil society representatives and international partners to strengthen Bangladesh’s capacity to monitor corruption trends and assess the impact of reform initiatives.
Over the two days, participants discussed international best practices, the operationalisation of the UNODC Statistical Framework to Measure Corruption, and ways to identify gaps, opportunities and priorities for improving corruption measurement and collaboration in Bangladesh.
Around 40 experts from relevant institutions reviewed existing data sources, including household surveys, administrative records and transparency assessments, to help build a comprehensive evidence base for ongoing national reforms.
The opening high-level session was attended by Anti-Corruption Commission Chairman Justice AKM Asaduzzaman as the chief guest.
In his speech, he stressed that sustainable anti-corruption reforms require collective commitment, adding that strong institutions, effective oversight, public participation and a culture of integrity are essential to building a society free from corruption.
Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics Director Md Emdadul Haque, who attended as a special guest, said the BBS remained committed to supporting national efforts to strengthen the evidence base for development and governance reforms within its mandate, and, where necessary, in collaboration with relevant institutions.
Swiss Ambassador to Bangladesh Reto Renggli said addressing corruption requires a collective shift in attitudes and mindsets, beginning in kindergartens and classrooms.
“Following rules is one thing, believing in the rules is a social precondition,” he said.
Norwegian Ambassador to Bangladesh Håkon Arald Gulbrandsen said Bangladesh would be among the first countries to implement the UNODC Statistical Framework to Measure Corruption if the initiative moves forward, describing it as a positive and practical step that would attract international attention.
UN Resident Coordinator a.i. Max Tunon underscored the strategic importance of measuring corruption and assessing the effectiveness of anti-corruption efforts for good governance, sustainable development and public trust in institutions.
He reaffirmed the UN system’s commitment to implementing the United Nations Convention against Corruption (UNCAC) and relevant resolutions of the Conference of the States Parties, particularly those related to corruption measurement.
He also stressed the importance of strengthening evidence-based public policies through the adoption of the UNODC statistical framework to demonstrate the actual impact of anti-corruption efforts in Bangladesh.
Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) Executive Director Iftekharuzzaman highlighted the need to strengthen institutional capacity to generate credible corruption-related data.
“The problem in Bangladesh is often not so much the generation of data, as the lack of interest and commitment to use the available data and knowledge that already exist on corruption,” he said.
He also called for exploring innovative approaches to measuring the comparative implications of the multi-trillion-dollar global money-laundering economy for source and host economies.
Dr Sofie Schuette, principal adviser at the U4 Anti-Corruption Resource Centre at the Chr Michelsen Institute, and Shah Mohammad Naheeaan, head of office at UNODC, also attended the high-level session.
Schuette stressed the importance of data in driving reforms, saying credible evidence could help Bangladesh translate anti-corruption commitments into meaningful change by guiding reforms, strengthening accountability and making progress measurable.
The workshop concluded on Tuesday with panel reflections from representatives of key oversight bodies and development partners on establishing sustainable accountability mechanisms.

item.title: Conspiracy or survival? Garment workers respond to allegations
item.description:
Garment workers demanding a minimum wage of Tk30,000 have rejected allegations of political incitement and a wider conspiracy behind their ongoing movement, insisting that soaring living costs, rather than any external influence, have driven them to protest.
The allegations surfaced as more than 100 people, including workers and police personnel, were injured in repeated clashes across industrial areas of Dhaka and Gazipur on Tuesday.
Police arrested 40 people accused of inciting unrest, claiming that outsiders had infiltrated the demonstrations.
Some police officials and labour leaders have alleged that politically motivated groups, including elements linked to the Awami League, are attempting to exploit the movement to create instability.
However, no independently verified evidence establishing such involvement has been presented.
Workers have strongly disputed the allegations, arguing that their struggle is rooted in economic hardship and that attempts to portray the movement as a conspiracy risk undermining their legitimate demands.
“We know nothing about any conspiracy. The high cost of living is hitting our stomachs. We are protesting out of sheer necessity to survive,” a worker in Mirpur said.
The workers maintain that the government’s formation of a wage board is insufficient to resolve the crisis.
They have vowed to continue demonstrating until a concrete announcement on a wage increase is made.
Shoeb Islam, a garment worker participating in the protests in Mirpur, told Bangla Tribune that workers had no involvement in sabotage or politically motivated violence.
“We, the workers, are not involved in any acts of sabotage. If anyone engages in such acts, it is a matter for the police to address,” he said.
He also alleged that police had unjustly attacked protesters and warned that workers would resist any arbitrary arrests of their colleagues.
Another worker, Shefali Begum, dismissed allegations that the demonstrations were being orchestrated by outside groups.
“We have not been incited by anyone. We are protesting for our own legitimate demands,” she said.
She argued that the police should identify and take action against any outsiders attempting to exploit the movement rather than holding ordinary workers responsible.
“If someone else has infiltrated the group with a different agenda, that is a matter for the police to address. It is unfair to blame the movement of ordinary workers for that,” she said.
Shefali said workers would no longer accept assurances without a specific announcement on wages.
“The government should engage in discussions and implement our demands. Only when there is an official announcement of a wage increase will we return to work,” she said.
Another worker, Shamim, said the government could bring the demonstrations to an immediate end by announcing the demanded minimum wage.
“If the government announces a minimum wage of Tk30,000, all the workers will return to their factories, and no one will remain on the streets,” he said.
Law enforcement officials, however, have maintained that individuals with motives unrelated to workers’ wage demands have infiltrated the demonstrations.
Md Mostafizur Rahman, deputy inspector general of Dhaka Range, said police had arrested 40 people in connection with unrest in Dhaka, Gazipur and Narayanganj, claiming that none of those detained were garment workers.
“Taking advantage of the workers’ legitimate movement, certain miscreants have infiltrated their ranks to stir up chaos,” he told journalists on Tuesday after visiting industrial facilities in Ashulia.
He said police were gathering evidence to identify those allegedly responsible for instigating violence.
Dhaka District Superintendent of Police Shamima Parveen also alleged that individuals wearing burqas and helmets had been inciting workers in an attempt to destabilise the country.
She claimed police had information about the financing of these activities but did not publicly disclose supporting evidence.
Meanwhile, Hasan Mohammad Nasher Rikabdar, deputy commissioner of Mirpur Division, questioned the motives of those continuing to demonstrate despite the formation of a wage board.
“Those currently involved in the protests are not workers. The government has already established a board to address wage increases for workers, and pay will indeed rise,” he said.
He warned that police would take firm action against anyone attempting to create disorder.
Some labour leaders have also raised concerns about alleged third-party involvement, while acknowledging the legitimacy of workers’ wage demands.
Nazma Akter, president of the Sommilito Garments Sromik Federation, said the formation of a wage board was a positive step and urged workers to return to their factories.
She alleged that certain groups were attempting to exploit the movement for their own interests.
“While the workers’ demands are legitimate, can acts of arson, looting and vandalism ever be a solution?” she asked.
Taslima Akter, president of Bangladesh Garment Workers Solidarity, similarly alleged that outside groups were inciting unrest.
“Some groups are exploiting these protests for their own benefit; there is clear incitement,” she said.
Both leaders urged workers to remain calm and allow the wage board to complete its work.
The dispute over the nature of the movement unfolded against a backdrop of escalating violence across several industrial areas.
In Mirpur, garment workers began leaving factories on Tuesday morning and attempted to occupy roads. Police used batons, tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse them, while some protesters responded by throwing bricks and stones.
Several rounds of clashes followed, leaving workers and police personnel injured. At Kalshi intersection, a police officer identified as Saymon was reportedly assaulted.
In Gazipur, workers repeatedly blocked sections of the Dhaka-Tangail and Dhaka-Mymensingh highways, triggering confrontations with police and causing severe traffic disruption.
There were also allegations that some BNP activists carrying sticks were present during the unrest, apparently seeking to suppress the demonstrations. Their involvement could not be independently verified.
Blockades in Gazipur and Narayanganj left passenger buses, trucks and other vehicles stranded for hours, causing widespread hardship for commuters.
Despite the violence, arrests and allegations of outside interference, protesting workers insisted that their central demand remained unchanged: a minimum wage of Tk30,000.
They said the movement would continue until the government announced a definite wage increase, maintaining that their struggle was about survival, not politics.

item.title: Tahsif murder: Police seek answers to Dip's 20-minute absence
item.description:
Investigators probing the death of former Air Force official Tahsif Souri are now focusing on a crucial 15- to 20-minute period on the night he went missing.
Police are trying to establish where Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip, a junior friend of Tahsif, was during that period and whom he contacted while they were at Nest Bar and Restaurant in Uttara before Tahsif's death.
Investigators said they obtained some important information during Dip's first four-day remand, but several questions remain unanswered.
Police have yet to establish where Tahsif was killed, the motive behind the murder or whether anyone else was involved. Despite the emergence of several important pieces of evidence and information over the past week, the circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear.
To find answers to these questions, the naval police have taken Dip into custody for a second round of remand, this time for three days.
On Tuesday, November 3, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Hasan Shahadat granted the three-day remand.
Earlier, Inspector Firoz Uddin of the Naval Police's Tongi outpost, the investigation officer in the case, had sought a further seven-day remand, citing eight reasons. The court granted three days.
Naval Police chief and Additional Inspector General Rezaul Karim told Dhaka Tribune: “The investigation is ongoing. We have obtained some important information. Further questioning is necessary. That is why Dip has been taken on remand for a second time.”
According to investigation sources, police are closely examining the movements of Dip and a young woman close to Tahsif before his death.
The remand application states that Dip had briefly left the premises while they were at Nest Bar and Restaurant. Investigators want to establish where he was during those 15 to 20 minutes and whom he contacted.
The police application states that it is necessary to examine where Dip went and whom he contacted after leaving the restaurant while he was with the victim.
Although investigators consider his movements during this period significant, no confirmed information has been disclosed about his whereabouts or communications.
The investigating officer said in the remand application submitted to the court that Dip had provided some important information during the first round of questioning.
However, the information is still being verified.
The officer alleged that Dip was “extremely cunning” and had tactfully avoided answering several questions during interrogation, while remaining silent on others.
The application said further intensive questioning was necessary for this reason.
The investigator's claims have raised fresh questions about what information Dip provided during the first round of questioning, how much of it matched physical evidence, CCTV footage and witness statements, and which inconsistencies remain unresolved.
Police have not disclosed details of the information obtained during the first round of questioning, citing the interests of the investigation.
Although Tahsif's body was recovered from the Turag River, investigators have yet to establish where he was killed.
The second remand application submitted to the court cited the need to determine the location of the murder and gather information about the motive.
Naval police recovered Tahsif's floating body from the Rajabari Ghat area of the Turag River on the afternoon of October 28.
The previous evening, October 27, Tahsif had left his home in Uttara after receiving a call from Dip.
Police are analysing CCTV footage, mobile phone call detail records (CDRs) and other evidence to reconstruct the sequence of events.
Dip, Tahsif's junior friend, has been under scrutiny since the investigation began.
On October 29, Dip said they had dinner together at a restaurant before parting ways near Uttara House Building.
However, investigation sources later said Dip had admitted to accompanying Tahsif to the Mazar Basti area of Tongi late at night.
Based on information provided by Dip, police recovered Tahsif's motorcycle from the area on the morning of October 30.
The recovery has raised questions about whether Dip's initial account matches the information subsequently obtained by investigators.
The naval police cited eight reasons in their application seeking a second round of remand for Dip.
These include verifying collected CCTV footage in his presence, examining his movements and communications during the 15- to 20-minute period at Nest Bar and Restaurant, and collecting and analysing the CDRs of Tahsif, Dip and other people involved in the case.
The application also cited the need to uncover the motive behind the murder, identify and arrest other unidentified suspects, recover evidence, gather information about the motive and establish the location of the killing.
According to the investigation officer, information gathered so far indicates that Tahsif was seen with Dip and the young woman before his death, visiting different places and eating at various restaurants.
As Tahsif was last seen with them, investigators suspect they may have some involvement in the case, the application said.
Female friend also on remand as police examine final hours
A female friend of Tahsif has also been arrested in the murder case.
On Sunday, November 1, the court granted police permission to take her on a four-day remand.
Investigators said the woman was seen with Tahsif at a bar in Uttara on the night of the incident.
Police are now focusing on verifying the statements of the two people who were with Tahsif before his death and reconstructing their movements that night.
Tahsif's father, KM Enayetul Karim, filed a murder case against unidentified individuals at Uttarkhan police station in Dhaka on the night of October 30.
Dip was shown arrested in the case on the same day. The following day, a court sent him to a four-day remand.

item.title: Mirpur people gripped by fear after three days of clashes
item.description:
People in Mirpur are living in fear amid a tense atmosphere as clashes between garment workers and police over the demand for a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000 have continued for three consecutive days.
Repeated chases and counter-chases between workers and police have turned parts of the area into virtual battlegrounds, spreading panic across Mirpur-10, Mirpur-2, Mirpur-14 and Mirpur-11. Many people are avoiding going outdoors unless absolutely necessary.
The situation emerged during visits to the area and conversations with local people on Tuesday.
Abu Hanif, a resident of the Purabi area in Mirpur, told Bangla Tribune, “Since Sunday, this area has felt like a war zone. Before we can even wake up properly in the morning, the loud blasts of sound grenades and the pungent smell of tear gas make life unbearable.”
He said the area remained tense from morning until afternoon as workers and police chased each other through the streets.
“Many people are afraid to go outside. We are even worried about taking our children to school,” he added.
Another resident, Shariful Islam, said ordinary people were reluctant to leave their homes out of fear.
“Police are arresting protesters and entering alleys to question people. They are also detaining many people. This has spread panic across the area,” he said.
Kawser, a resident of Mirpur-2, said no one in the area was able to live peacefully amid the protests and clashes.
“Since clashes are taking place, a sense of fear has gripped everyone,” he said.
Housewife Sharifa Begum said, “We have to step outside in fear. Yesterday, I went out once but had to return home quickly. I have not been able to go out since. Fear has spread everywhere.”
During a visit, tea stalls inside neighbourhood alleys were found closed. Locals said law enforcement agencies had instructed shopkeepers to keep them shut. Several large roadside shops were also closed.
Garment workers have been demonstrating for several days, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. However, the movement turned violent on Sunday, when protesters set fire to a police vehicle.
Workers attempted to take to the streets again on Monday but were prevented by a strong police presence.
On Tuesday morning, fresh clashes broke out between police and workers at several locations. Police fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse protesters, while workers also attacked police. The situation eased somewhat after noon.
A police source said around six people accused of creating disorder were arrested on Monday. Eleven cases have been filed over clashes during the past two days, with more than 10,000 people named as accused.

item.title: BRRI develops high-yielding salt-tolerant rice variety
item.description:
The Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI) has developed a new high-yielding, salt-tolerant rice variety, BRRI Dhan 119, offering fresh prospects for rice production in the country's salinity-prone coastal regions.
Developed by BRRI's Plant Breeding Division with financial support from the Location-Specific Technology Development (LSTD) Project, the variety received final approval for transplanted Aman cultivation at the 116th meeting of the National Seed Board on October 28. It is also suitable for Boro cultivation, although final approval for the season is pending, researchers said.
The research team was led by Dr Mohammad Akhlasur Rahman, chief scientific officer of BRRI's Plant Breeding Division, with Dr Hasina Khatun, Nusrat Jahan, Armin Akter Setu and Ribet Farzana Disha as members.
BRRI Dhan 119 produces an average yield of 5.7 tonnes per hectare under suitable management conditions, with yields ranging from 4.8 to 7.6 tonns depending on salinity and environmental conditions. Research findings show that it produces approximately one tonnn more per hectare than BRRI Dhan 73. The variety has a growth duration of around 115 days and an average plant height of 113cm. Its strong stems make it resistant to lodging, while each panicle produces an average of 215 filled grains, around 70-80 more than BRRI Dhan 73. Its medium-slender, white grains produce fluffy, non-sticky rice when cooked.
One of its key characteristics is its ability to tolerate salinity at different growth stages. According to BRRI research data, it can withstand salinity levels of up to 12 deciSiemens per metre (dS/m) for three weeks during the seedling stage. It can also maintain yield potential at salinity levels of 8-10 dS/m during sensitive stages from vegetative growth to reproduction. Field trials in Cox's Bazar assessed its performance under fluctuating salinity conditions, while further evaluations were conducted in saline areas of Satkhira and favourable non-saline environments. Farmer-participatory trials were also carried out in different parts of the country. Researchers noted that actual yields would depend on salinity intensity, duration, crop growth stage and field management.
With a growth duration of around 115 days, the variety could help diversify cropping patterns in coastal areas. After harvesting Aman rice, farmers may have sufficient time to cultivate sunflower or salt-tolerant mustard on medium-high to high land
For Boro cultivation, Performance Yield Trials were completed at 20 locations across saline and non-saline environments under the supervision of the Seed Certification Agency. Based on the results, the National Technical Committee has recommended the variety for Boro cultivation. Final approval from the National Seed Board would allow farmers to grow it in both Aman and Boro seasons.
BRRI recommends sowing seeds between July 1 and July 30 for transplanted Aman cultivation. Seedlings aged 25-30 days should be transplanted, with two to three seedlings per hill and spacing of 20cm between rows and 15cm between hills. The recommended fertiliser doses per hectare are 234kg of urea, 87kg of TSP, 117kg of MOP, 78kg of gypsum and 12kg of zinc sulphate. The institute's Genetic Resources and Seed Division in Gazipur is responsible for seed production, while ensuring adequate supplies of quality seeds will be essential for expanding cultivation.
BRRI Director General Dr Rafiqul Islam said the variety demonstrated the advanced breeding capabilities of Bangladeshi agricultural scientists. "BRRI Dhan 119 will not only bring hope to farmers in salt-affected coastal areas but will also play an important role in strengthening our food security and increasing agricultural production and farmers' incomes," he said.
Dr Khandakar Md Iftekharuddaula , head of the Plant Breeding Division, described its development within seven and a half years as a significant achievement. Lead breeder Dr Mohammad Akhlasur Rahman said the research journey had been long and challenging, adding that seeing the benefits reach farmers' fields would be the team's greatest reward.
Dr Anwar Hossain, project director of the LSTD Project, said the variety was a significant achievement under the initiative. He added that BRRI Dhan 116, BRRI Dhan 117 and BRRI Hybrid Dhan 10 had previously been released under the project, reflecting its continued contribution to developing location-specific rice varieties for Bangladesh.

item.title: Govt asks officials, employees to keep ID cards visible inside Secretariat
item.description:
The government has instructed all officials and employees working at the Secretariat to keep their identity cards visible at all times while entering and staying inside the premises to strengthen security.
The Ministry of Home Affairs issued the directive on Tuesday, saying displaying identity cards was essential to reinforce security, control access and maintain overall discipline at the Secretariat.
It said different categories of visitors, including those attending meetings and entering through one-time passwords (OTPs), also visit the Secretariat, where Prime Minister Tarique Rahman now works every day.
Against this backdrop, displaying identity cards at all times has become particularly important to ensure internal security, the ministry said.
It urged all ministries and divisions to instruct their officials and employees to comply with the directive.
The latest instruction follows another order issued on October 27 to tighten control over visitors' entry into the Secretariat.
Under the earlier directive, the authorities asked officials to keep meetings with offices outside the Secretariat to a minimum on Mondays and Thursdays when visitor entry is suspended.
It also said visitor entry time had been shifted from noon to 2pm and that OTPs should be issued accordingly. General visitors were not to be issued more than one OTP a week.
The earlier notice was aimed at ensuring security at the Secretariat and improving the monitoring and supervision of visitors.

item.title: Landless people demand rehabilitation before development
item.description:
A meeting of landless people was held at Rangpur Public Library Ground on Tuesday organised by Bangladesh Landless Movement, with a three-point demand, including rehabilitation before development.
The meeting placed three key demands - rehabilitation of landless people, ensuring their access to government-owned khas land and establishing a discrimination-free society.
Advocate Hasnat Kaiyum, chief adviser of the Bangladesh Landless Movement and president of the Bangladesh State Reform Movement, attended the meeting as the chief guest.
He called for a special tribunal to prosecute those involved in looting and siphoning off national wealth abroad. He also demanded the recovery of laundered assets and reforms to make the state more accountable to citizens.
Speaking at the function, the organisation's General Secretary Sheikh Nasir Uddin demanded landless cards for all landless people, reserved parliamentary seats for them and the formation of an independent Land and Agricultural Reform Commission.
Presiding over the meeting, Divisional Coordinator Kanak Rahman called for priority-based rehabilitation of landless people in Rangpur and the creation of employment opportunities through industrialisation and agricultural development.
Other speakers demanded the inclusion of landless representatives in khas land distribution committees and the recovery of illegally occupied government land for allocation to genuine landless families and farmers.
The leaders warned of a nationwide movement if their demands were not met.
Following the meeting, participants brought out a procession through Rangpur city and submitted memorandums to the Rangpur City Corporation administrator and the deputy commissioner.

item.title: No Rash Mela at Dublar Char, 3-day religious event set for Nov 22–24
item.description:
The traditional Rash Mela at Dublar Char in the Sundarbans will not be held this year, marking the fifth consecutive year of suspension since 2021. However, a three-day programme featuring Rash Purnima Puja and the sacred ritual bath, known as Punya Snan, will be held from November 22 to 24 exclusively for followers of the Sanatan (Hindu) faith.
To ensure pilgrims’ safety, the Forest Department has designated five river routes to Dublar Char. Personnel from the Forest Department, police, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and Coast Guard will patrol the waterways during the programme.
Rezaul Karim Chowdhury, divisional forest officer of the Sundarbans East Division, confirmed that the fair would remain suspended this year. He said followers of the Sanatan faith could obtain entry passes and permits from the Forest Department to attend the religious ceremonies, provided they complied with all official instructions.
Entry passes will be issued for November 22–24 upon payment of prescribed fees, which will vary according to vessel type, number of passengers and duration of stay. Applicants must submit a photocopy of their national identity card (NID).
Pilgrims must begin their journey together from designated departure points during daylight hours on November 22 and return collectively on November 24. Independent travel will not be permitted.
Vessels will be allowed to operate only during daylight hours and may stop exclusively at designated Forest Department checkposts. Each vessel must carry an adequate number of life jackets or lifebuoys and clearly display its registration number and passenger count.
Pilgrims must retain their entry tokens throughout their stay and carry either their original NID or a certificate issued by their Union Parishad chairman. All vessels must report to the control room at Alorkol.
The carriage of firearms, explosives, hunting equipment, single-use plastics, loudspeakers and fireworks is strictly prohibited. Violations of the regulations may result in legal action.
Imran Ahmed, conservator of forests for the Sundarbans, said patrols had been intensified to prevent deer poaching during the period.
The Rash Mela was first introduced in 1923 by Sadhu Haribhajan. Although the traditional fair has remained suspended since 2021, the religious rituals have continued to take place annually.
