item.title: Government: There are challenges, but the people’s govt will not be defeated
item.description:
1

The fall and flight of the Sheikh Hasina regime represent the victory of a single battle, but the broader war is far from over. The ongoing struggle is a much longer one—a journey towards building a state rooted in equality, human dignity, and social justice. Whichever party had assumed power following the 13th Jatiya Sangsad (national parliamentary election) would have inherited the monumental challenge of rebuilding a devastated state apparatus. During the mafia-like, prolonged rule of the Awami League, Bangladesh’s state institutions were rendered so ineffective that, in many instances, they were left near total collapse.

Many draw comparisons between Bangladesh’s current predicament and Sri Lanka’s economic recovery or Nepal’s political transition. This comparison, however, is not appropriate. To truly comprehend the situation in Bangladesh, one should look instead to the experiences of Tunisia or other Middle Eastern nations that navigated the Arab Spring. Much like those countries, Bangladesh endured a prolonged period of authoritarian rule during which virtually every state institution was systematically dismantled to maintain power.

A democratic state is not merely about holding elections or changing governments. It functions through a network of institutions, rules, and established structures. The judiciary, the executive, and the administration must operate independently within their respective mandates and jurisdictions. For a long time, this system ceased to function in Bangladesh. As a result, the incumbent government must simultaneously tackle complex political, economic, and administrative challenges—restoring state institutions to working order while meeting the immense expectations of the public.

2

Through the July Mass Uprising, the public voiced a profound desire to establish a democratic Bangladesh. For ordinary citizens, democracy begins with the unhindered right to vote. People want an electoral system through which they can freely choose their preferred representatives and government, applying this right to local government as well. Citizens also expect their elected government to oversee their general welfare. Furthermore, the conscious section of society places great emphasis on freedom of expression, human rights, judicial independence, and the effective functioning of state bodies. These constitute the fundamental prerequisites of a democratic state.

In evaluating the government’s performance over the past eight months, these expectations must be kept in mind. It cannot be denied that in certain areas, progress has fallen short of public expectation. However, one must consider the conditions under which the government assumed office.

In working alongside the administration, I have observed that a large section of the bureaucracy lacks experience in serving a government formed through participatory elections. An elected government comes with an electoral manifesto, and the civil service must relearn how to align its operations to implement that mandate. Nevertheless, I believe the process of gradually restoring state institutions to efficacy has commenced; it remains a long-term undertaking.

Significant shifts have also occurred regarding political rights and freedom of speech. Opposition political parties and ordinary citizens now freely offer sharp criticism of the government. At times, certain statements may seem to cross the boundary of acceptability, yet the government receives them with tolerance. In a democratic framework, such tolerance is vital.

3

In a country like Bangladesh, the economy remains the paramount priority. When citizens experience crises in their livelihoods and earnings, other national challenges feel magnified. Even the most efficient government faces ongoing issues, but during economic hardship, the burden of these problems weighs much more heavily on the populace.

At present, the primary economic challenge stems from the fallout of the egregious plundering that occurred under Awami rule, now further compounded by the global situation. Conflict in the Middle East has triggered a global energy crisis. Bangladesh has encountered this shock at a time when, for years, insufficient efforts were made to develop domestic energy resources. Under the Hasina administration, necessary steps to explore and develop national energy assets were neglected. Consequently, when instability strikes international energy markets, Bangladesh pays a steep price.

In response, the government is striving to secure long-term energy security on one hand, while taking immediate measures to support poor and vulnerable communities on the other. Plans are underway to distribute “Family Cards” to 4.1 million households within the current financial year. Estimating an average of five members per family, approximately 20 million people stand to benefit, with each family receiving monthly assistance of Tk 2,500. Additionally, the scope of the VGF (Vulnerable Group Feeding) and food assistance programmes has been expanded, with rice allocations doubled in certain cases. We hope these measures will alleviate the hardship of those facing economic distress.

To ensure energy security, initiatives have been launched to explore and drill new gas fields, with efforts focused on swiftly utilising the gas discovered in Bhola. The government is also prioritising solar energy, introducing incentives and policy measures so citizens can easily generate, consume, and sell surplus solar power from their homes. Legislation regarding solar energy is currently being drafted.

The benefits of these measures will not materialise overnight. However, once the energy crisis is substantially managed, it will yield a positive knock-on effect across other sectors of the economy, boosting investment and creating widespread employment.

4

In evaluating the law and order situation, one must recall how the police force was utilised prior to 5 August. Under the Hasina regime, the police underwent a form of militarisation—a complete departure from how law enforcement functions in a democratic state.

Recovering from the state the police found themselves in after 5 August was no easy task. My assessment is that the police are performing significantly better today. The transformation is stark when compared to the period under the interim government, when lawlessness frequently flared up, with groups taking the law into their own hands. Public singing was suppressed; women were prevented from playing football; traditional folk theatre (Jatra), fairs, and cultural activities were routinely disrupted. Shrines faced dreadful violence, with over a hundred shrines vandalised and set ablaze. Even the offices of the country’s leading newspapers, such as Prothom Alo and The Daily Star, were targeted with explicit threats and arson while the government remained passive.

Present-day Bangladesh has almost entirely emerged from that chaotic climate. Isolated incidents still occur—and they should not—but overall law and order has improved markedly.

Nevertheless, it is natural for the public to hold high expectations for a government that secured a two-thirds majority in parliament and the backing of over half the electorate. Measured against those high standards, some may feel that law and order has not improved sufficiently. A democratic government must respect and address these public concerns. I am confident that we will achieve substantial progress in short order.

5

It cannot be denied that allegations of extortion and illegal land occupation under the guise of political affiliations continue to surface. However, one must recognise that these problems are deeply entrenched in Bangladesh. Expecting every societal malady to vanish the day after a tyrannical regime is overthrown through a mass uprising is unrealistic. Reversing a political and social culture built over decades requires time.

The crucial issue here is whether the government is actively confronting these problems and whether conditions are improving. Positive precedents have already been set: a Member of Parliament and a Minister of State were obliged to step down from their positions—one facing allegations of land grabbing, and the other having publicly breached the law.

This sends an unmistakable signal to the public that the government will not turn a blind eye to wrongdoing. Work is currently underway to identify extortion and other illegal activities at the grassroots level, and further action will follow. Given the depth of the issue, sustained and methodical effort is required.

6

Certain concerns have been raised by civil society, human rights activists, and relevant stakeholders regarding various laws enacted by the government. Discussion and debate on these matters are welcome and necessary. However, when assessing these laws, one key principle should be kept in mind: we must not evaluate every piece of legislation solely through the lens of our experience under the Sheikh Hasina administration.

Assuming that a law will be abused in the future simply because past laws were misused is an erroneous conclusion. Even the best law can be weaponised by a government intent on harassment, but the existence of scope for misuse does not mean a government will inevitably exploit it. Alongside statutory provisions, practical application is paramount. Beyond the mere wording of the law, a government’s political goodwill and accountability are what truly matter.

If the application of any law infringes upon civil rights or leads to harassment, citizens must question it, and the law should be amended where necessary.

The defining hallmark of a democratic government is its readiness to acknowledge mistakes and rectify them. That is where the strength of democracy lies. A government will not always make the right decision, but it must possess the mindset to correct its course when errors occur. From rebuilding state institutions to steering the economy, maintaining law and order, and safeguarding civil rights, we must continuously nurture this democratic tradition. A government elected by the mandate of the people, marching forward hand-in-hand with its citizens, will not fail in this endeavor.

* Adviser to the Prime Minister on Policy and Strategy, Information and Broadcasting, and Culture

item.title: Garment worker injured in Gazipur protests dies; around 50 factories shut
item.description:
A readymade garment worker who was critically injured during protests in Gazipur over demands for higher wages has died. Toufiq Sheikh, 21, died while undergoing treatment at Shin-Shin Japan Hospital in Uttara, Dhaka, on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, more than 50 garment factories in Gazipur announced closures last night amid workers’ unrest and instability in the industrial belt. Some factories have announced a one-day closure, while others will remain shut for two to three days.

Toufiq was the son of Tabibur Rahman Tabi Khan of Chhaygharia village in Gobindaganj upazila of Gaibandha. He lived in the Banglabazar area of Gazipur and worked at the local Laila Garments factory.

Toufiq’s relatives said he had been living in the Banglabazar area and working in garment factories for around five years. On Monday, while a workers’ protest was under way in front of Noman Group’s Territory Garments factory, Toufiq tried to record an attack on his mobile phone. At that point, the attackers turned on him and beat him up, leaving him critically injured. Fellow workers rescued him and admitted him to hospital, where he died yesterday morning while receiving treatment.

However, Mohammad Belayet Hossain, additional commissioner (crime and operations) of Gazipur Metropolitan Police (GMP), said some outsiders had gone to a factory and pressured the authorities to shut it down. When the factory management refused, the outsiders clashed with the workers, leaving one worker critically injured. He later died.

No police personnel were present at the scene during the incident, he added.

Hopes of calm after factory closures

More than 50 garment factories in Gazipur have announced closures amid workers’ unrest and instability in the industrial belt. The information was confirmed by separate notices issued by factory authorities last night.

Cotton Club (BD) Ltd. and Cotton Cloud (BD) Ltd. in the Kashimpur area of Gazipur have jointly announced a two-day general holiday. Their notices said the factories would remain closed today, Wednesday, and tomorrow, Thursday, in view of workers’ unrest, workplace instability and overall security risks in various industrial areas across the country over the determination and implementation of the minimum wage structure for the garment industry. However, employees of the security and maintenance departments will be exempt from the closure.

Meanwhile, Lee Fashion Industry Ltd. in Purba Chandra, Kaliakair upazila, has announced a one-day general holiday. According to a notice issued by its human resources management department, the relevant sections of all shifts will remain closed today. All shifts will resume normal operations on Thursday (5 November).

In addition, Panorama Apparels Ltd. in the Bhogra area of Gazipur city, Mitali Club and Jockey Garments in Kashimpur have announced three-day closures. Standard Group in Jarun, Konabari, has declared a two-day holiday. Montex and DBL have also announced two-day closures.

Apex Holdings Ltd. in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair upazila has announced a one-day closure. More than 50 factories, including Ecotex Ltd., Cocola Food Products, Sadma Fashion, Hydroxide Ltd. and Interstoff in the same area, have also announced closures. Some of these factories will remain shut for one day, while others have opted for two days.

Jahangir Alam, an official of Lee Fashion, said the factory had been closed for two days because of workers’ unrest. As Friday is the weekly holiday, workers will get three consecutive days off. They hope the situation will return to normal during this period, he added.

Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Md Amzad Hossain said they had so far received reports of several factories being closed. However, they had also learnt that the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) had announced that factories should not be closed.

item.title: When rising prices become a constant burden
item.description:
A review of several old newspapers suggests that the first report on market prices in Bangladesh after independence was published by the state-owned daily Dainik Bangla.

Published on 27 December 1971, the report was headlined, “Prices of Fish, Eggs and Vegetables Fall in Dhaka.” It began:

“Since normal life resumed across Bangladesh, including the capital Dhaka, and communication systems were restored, the supply of various commodities to the city has been increasing day by day. As a result, prices of different goods have also begun to fall rapidly. These include vegetables, fish, eggs, meat and other items.”

The next report on market prices in Dainik Bangla appeared 22 days later, on 19 January 1972. This time, the news was quite the opposite. The headline read, “Commodity Prices Rising, Greed for Excessive Profits the Main Reason.” The report began:

“Prices of essential commodities in daily life have risen abnormally in recent times. The prices of some items have already soared to such heights that they are on the verge of moving beyond the purchasing power of the public. Traders cite supply constraints as the reason for rising prices. Using the seemingly compelling argument that supply is lower than demand, they have been raising prices in accordance with the principles of economics.

 “There is no doubt that supplies of some commodities in the market are inadequate. This is only natural for war-ravaged Bangladesh. But a slight shortage in supply does not justify selling kerosene, which used to cost Tk 6.50, for Tk 24. There is no other legitimate explanation for this apart from the greed for excessive profits. There is also no doubt that the greed of traders hoarding goods is at work. Otherwise, why should prices soar when goods are available in the market?

“It is not only the price of kerosene, an essential everyday item, that has risen. Prices have increased for rice, lentils, mustard oil, soap, baby food, cigarettes, matches, blades and a wide range of other goods. And these are not merely marginal increases. Prices have doubled or even tripled.”

That was how it began. Over the next 55 years, prices in the country continued to rise. Sometimes the pace was slow, at other times rapid. A look at budget speeches shows that finance ministers have devoted more attention to inflation and the cost of living than to almost any other issue. They have had fewer success stories to tell and more failures to acknowledge.

Of course, expenses have not been the only thing to rise. People’s incomes have also increased. The economy has expanded, growth has taken place and per capita income has risen. But incomes have failed to keep pace with expenses. As a result, the rising cost of living has become a constant economic reality for ordinary people in this country. Everyone has felt why economists call inflation a silent killer.

2

The rising cost of living is not a problem unique to Bangladesh. There are also many examples of hyperinflation, a phenomenon known in economic theory as hyperinflation. Generally, when inflation exceeds 50 per cent in a single month, it is classified as hyperinflation.

Hungary experienced the worst hyperinflation in the world. The situation became so dire that, in July 1946, prices were doubling on average every 15 hours. In Germany, monthly inflation stood at around 29,500 per cent in October 1923. In Zimbabwe, monthly inflation reached 79.6 billion per cent in November 2008. In Yugoslavia, it was around 313 million per cent in January 1994. Venezuela recorded annual inflation of around 130,000 per cent in 2018, while prices in Argentina rose by 196.6 per cent in a single month in July 1989.

The United States experienced a prolonged period of high inflation from 1965 to 1982. In 1974, then President Gerald Ford called inflation “Public Enemy Number One”.

Rising prices make everyday life difficult for people. The pressure does not merely cause public hardship; it can also put the state at risk. A 2011 study found just that. Titled Food Prices and Political Instability, the study analysed data from more than 120 countries between 1970 and 2007.

It found that rising food prices weakened democratic institutions in low-income countries and increased the risk of protests, riots and conflict. When food prices rise, life becomes harder for poor people. That pressure combines with other grievances and fuels instability.

This does not happen only in low-income and developing countries. The protests seen across Europe, including in France, have also been driven by the rising cost of living. There is no need to look that far away. The student-led mass uprising in Bangladesh in July and August 2024 was also influenced by the rising cost of living.

In 2025, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) published a fact-finding report on human rights violations during the student-led movement. The report cited a sense of deprivation of economic and social rights, inequality, corruption and a lack of employment opportunities for young people as factors behind the protests. It also said: “Since 2022, low- and middle-income Bangladeshis have been disproportionately affected by food and fuel inflation.”

3

Bangladesh is now experiencing its longest economic slowdown since 1990. People are living amid high inflation, low employment and slowing economic growth. There is an economic term for this situation: stagflation.

Since 2022, prices of essential commodities in the country have continued to rise. But incomes and wages have not increased at the same rate. According to data from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), the Consumer Price Index rose by around 54 per cent between September 2021 and September 2026.

Over the same period, the Wage Rate Index increased by around 45 per cent. In other words, although wages have risen, they have failed to keep pace with the rising cost of living.

The pressure has been greatest on families with little savings, uncertain incomes or outstanding debts. According to a 2025 estimate by the Power and Participation Research Centre (PPRC), around 18 per cent of households are still above the poverty line but remain at risk of falling into poverty if their incomes decline or expenses rise.

The World Bank’s 2025 Bangladesh Poverty and Equity Assessment report points to a similar risk. It says that in 2022, 36 per cent of the country’s population, or around 62 million people, were just above the poverty line. They had little savings, uncertain consumption expenditure and inadequate social protection. As a result, they too risk falling into poverty if their incomes decline or expenses increase.

According to the World Bank report, as inflation outpaces wage growth, the poverty rate could rise from 18.7 per cent in 2022 to 21.2 per cent in 2025.

To understand this pressure, consider a family of four. Suppose their monthly income was Tk 20,000 in September 2021.

According to the BBS Consumer Price Index, prices of goods and services had risen by around 54 per cent by September 2026 compared with that time. The same basket of goods that could be bought for Tk 20,000 then would now cost around Tk 30,800.

Over the same period, the Wage Rate Index increased by around 45 per cent. If the family’s income had risen at that rate, it would now stand at Tk 29,000. But they would need Tk 30,800 to make the same purchases as before. That would leave them with a monthly shortfall of around Tk 1,800. In other words, although wages have increased, they have failed to keep pace with the rising cost of living.

At the request of the National Pay Commission, the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) conducted a survey titled Living Standard Survey 2025. Data for the survey were collected between 14 and 18 September 2025. It found that 47.42 per cent of households had borrowed money to meet essential expenses in the 12 months preceding the survey.

4

A study titled Governing for Growth? Economic Performance and Finance Minister Survival in Democracies and Autocracies was published in 2026. It was conducted by Jonas Villibaldi Schmidt of the University of Oslo in Norway and Jacob Nirup of Stockholm University in Sweden.

Analysing data on more than 2,800 finance ministers between 1966 and 2021, the researchers found that finance ministers in democracies are more likely to remain in office when the economy performs well and face a greater risk of being removed during crises. However, they found no relationship between economic conditions and changes in finance ministers in autocratic countries.

The study Inflation Surprises and Election Outcomes was conducted by three German professors—Jonathan Färberle, Kathrin Mohr and Moritz Schularick. The researchers analysed 365 elections in 18 developed countries since 1948.

According to their findings, when inflation is 10 percentage points higher than expected, support for opposition radical, populist and mainstream political parties could increase by an average of 15 per cent. This trend was more pronounced when prices rose faster than wages.

Taken together, these findings suggest that inflationary pressure and the rising cost of living have a political economy of their own. The question is: how well do our politicians understand this reality when they are in power?

5

The big question facing the country at this moment is whether the crisis will ease soon. The International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) forecast offers little reason for optimism. The finance minister has said people will have to wait another two years.

But will ordinary voters, who elected the government with a huge mandate, be willing to wait that long? How many people could fall below the poverty line during this period? And how much further could the middle class be squeezed?

Controlling inflation while overcoming the investment slowdown will not be easy. Nevertheless, this is what needs to be done, and it is what people expect. But how well-equipped are we with the economic plans, implementation capacity, strong institutions and good governance needed to fulfil these expectations?

* Shawkat Hossain, Head of Online, Prothom Alo

item.title: Democrats capture Congress in sweeping setback for Trump
item.description:
• Democrats on track to capture House and Senate

  • Democratic gains reach deep into Trump strongholds

Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and House on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories that reached deep into Republican strongholds as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump.

The size and breadth of the Democratic wave were still coming into focus, but the party prevailed in states long thought to be out of reach, including conservative bastions like South Carolina, Texas and Iowa.

The Democratic wave underscored voters’ deep frustration with Trump’s stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war against Iran in February, which drove gas prices up sharply. In poll after poll, voters expressed anxiety about the cost of living and anger at the way Trump has handled the issue.

In Kansas, Adam Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat since the Great Depression nearly a century ago.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown claimed a seat that belonged to Vice President JD Vance two years ago, while Texas Democratic state Representative James Talarico withstood a barrage of outside spending to defeat scandal-plagued Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Both Ohio and Texas voted for Trump by a double-digit margin in 2024.

In South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, pediatrician Annie Andrews triumphed over Republican Senator Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat after the death of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.

Trump elevated Paxton and Graham ahead of more established candidates despite clear liabilities. Paxton has been at the center of a litany of controversies, including his 2023 impeachment and securities fraud charges, while Graham’s admitted inexperience drew negative headlines.

Trump campaigned heavily for Paxton, Graham and Ohio’s Jon Husted as part of a late election blitz that included more than two dozen rallies, and the president told his supporters repeatedly to “pretend I’m on the ballot” in an effort to fire up his base.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter.”

Democrats had flipped six Republican Senate seats in all, ensuring a majority even if they don’t manage to hold their own seats in competitive Michigan and Minnesota.

Democrats were also on track to take control of the US House of Representatives after flipping at least eight Republican seats in states including Kentucky, New Jersey and North Carolina and showing strength even in solidly conservative districts.

The party’s dominance extended to other races as well. Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a three-term incumbent, lost to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, while Democrats also captured governorships in conservative Iowa and Ohio.

A rebuke to Trump, winner says

“In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump,” incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, the projected winner in Georgia, told supporters at a victory party.

In Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody fended off Democrat Angie Nixon but was ahead by only about 3 percentage points in a state Trump carried by 13 points in 2024, according to a vote count compiled by Reuters and USA Today, further evidence that even solidly Republican states were shifting dramatically toward Democrats.

Democrats held onto three House districts in Florida that Republican lawmakers had redrawn earlier this year, all of which backed Trump by at least 9 percentage points.

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70 per cent of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

item.title: Democracy and opposition politics in Bangladesh
item.description:
In discussions about the role of opposition parties—and, by extension, ruling parties—in protecting and consolidating democracy, we often avoid a fundamental question: What kind of democracy do we actually want to establish?

Democracy can take many forms. Free and fair elections mark only the beginning of a country's democratic journey. But even free and fair elections can produce two very different outcomes. On the one hand, power may become concentrated in the hands of a single party or individual, giving rise to a ‘tyranny of the majority’. On the other, a shift in the balance of power may produce an ‘aristocracy of the elite’, marginalising ordinary people. The fundamental challenge of democracy is to find the right balance between these two extremes. The ultimate goal is to ensure that the genuine voices and concerns of citizens are reflected in policymaking through their elected representatives. Therefore, what constitutes the ‘ideal’ role of an opposition party in a democracy depends on the kind of democratic framework we want to establish in the state.

For many in Bangladesh, the concept of democracy is extremely narrow. A country is considered ‘democratic’ as long as power changes hands through free and fair elections every five years. This minimalist definition of democracy cannot be dismissed as entirely wrong. However, if our attention remains focused solely on election day, expecting the opposition to play a constructive role in the intervening period becomes meaningless.

Under such an arrangement, elections may take place every five years, but in the period between two elections, all power remains concentrated in the hands of the ruling party. State institutions lose their independence, while citizens' role is reduced to casting their votes. Because of these structural weaknesses, the opposition has no meaningful opportunity to hold the executive accountable during the five-year term. Yet, every five years, it enters the race to form a government wielding enormous power.

Responsible behaviour cannot reasonably be expected from opposition parties within such an institutional framework.

By contrast, if we view democracy as a continuous process in which public policies are shaped through political dialogue and compromise, where no single actor can exercise absolute dominance and the executive is subject to rigorous oversight to prevent the abuse of power, opportunities emerge for the opposition to play an effective role.

Essentially, what we need is a representative liberal democracy that moves politics away from the ‘winner-takes-all’ principle towards a ‘something to win, something to lose’ approach.

These three forms of democracy—electoral, liberal-institutional and participatory—are not mutually exclusive. If free and fair elections are the foundation, the liberal-institutional framework is the shield against the abuse of power, while participatory mechanisms provide ordinary people with the means to exercise power.

However, no ruling party willingly agrees to limit its own power. Therefore, the opposition's primary responsibility should be to make the case for building such a political framework, forge alliances with civil society and put pressure on the government to undertake structural reforms.

Representative liberal democracy, however, has a major limitation of its own. It often becomes excessively dependent on elite bargaining and narrows the scope for ordinary people to directly influence policymaking.

In the name of allowing representatives to rise above narrow, constituency-based demands and make independent decisions in the national interest, citizens' opinions are often disregarded in practice.

This limitation has given rise to the idea of ‘participatory democracy’, which prioritises direct public involvement in decision-making. This approach can be transformative, with major policy decisions being made through citizens' assemblies or regular referendums. Alternatively, it can take the form of an effective consultative system through which citizens can easily communicate their demands to elected representatives.

Such participatory arrangements must, of course, be protected by constitutional safeguards to ensure that the rights of minorities are not undermined by the preferences of the majority. If we want to build a vibrant democracy of this kind, opposition parties must move closer to ordinary people.

These three forms of democracy—electoral, liberal-institutional and participatory—are not mutually exclusive. If free and fair elections are the foundation, the liberal-institutional framework is the shield against the abuse of power, while participatory mechanisms provide ordinary people with the means to exercise power.

Our greatest challenge is to bring these three dimensions together. The more we move beyond a narrowly ‘election-centric’ understanding of democracy towards involving citizens in policymaking, the more important the role of opposition parties becomes.

In the present context of Bangladesh, the opposition's role is particularly sensitive and urgent. When the ruling party is unwilling to rebuild democratic institutions, intolerant of criticism, busy politicising the bureaucracy, blurring the distinction between the party and the government, and failing to keep its own activists under control, it would be misguided to expect the ruling party to initiate reforms on its own. In the face of authoritarian tendencies, opposition parties must build a strong resistance by combining street mobilisation with civil society initiatives and develop a blueprint for an alternative political order to rein in the abuse of power.

The question is whether opposition parties in Bangladesh are fulfilling this responsibility under the present circumstances.

Unfortunately, opposition politics remains centred on confrontation and distant from citizen-oriented thinking. To establish progressive and constructive opposition politics, these parties need to focus on several specific priorities.

First, rather than limiting themselves to criticising government actions, opposition parties must clearly explain to the public the rationale for bringing about sustainable political and institutional reforms. They need to build a counter-reformist political bloc involving civil society and institutional stakeholders to challenge the ruling elite coalition.

Second, the traditional programmes of ‘long marches’ and displays of political strength have now reached the limits of their effectiveness.

Instead of merely gathering their own supporters, opposition parties must reach out to people from all walks of life. They must explain in clear and accessible language how everyday crises—including rising prices, unemployment, food insecurity and corruption—are products of the existing system of governance. Without this tireless and patient engagement, winning public trust will be impossible.

Third, opposition parties must have a clear vision for establishing an equitable society. Even if a party operates within a democratic framework, relying on populism, religious extremism or discriminatory attitudes will ultimately lead to a tyranny of the majority. Opposition parties must explicitly pledge to build a liberal political culture that protects the rights of every citizen, regardless of religion, ethnicity or gender identity, and respects differing opinions. No state can be a liberal democracy without protecting minority rights.

How successful are Bangladesh's current opposition parties in meeting these expectations?

Consider Jamaat-e-Islami, the country's largest opposition political force. The party appears more comfortable with confrontation and emotion-driven politics than with political compromise or objective reform proposals. Although it uses the word ‘reform’ as a politically appealing slogan, it simply avoids proposals that do not align with its ideology, such as women's political empowerment. Instead of presenting constructive alternative policies, it continues to rely on strategies dating back to the 1990s.

At the same time, the kind of society Jamaat envisions is fundamentally at odds with the idea of a liberal democratic state. Although the party claims to have substantial female leadership within its ranks, it remains silent on nominating women candidates in elections. It has failed miserably to win the confidence of religious and political minorities.

Historically, the party has struggled to accept the reality that Bangladesh, despite having a Muslim majority, is fundamentally a universal democratic republic in which the majority cannot impose its views by force. As a matter of political opportunism, it is eager to deepen cultural divisions in society and ride the wave of right-wing populism. Consequently, its vision for change is by no means inclusive.

The position of the relatively young National Citizen Party (NCP), by contrast, is somewhat different. It has a genuine commitment to institutional reforms, and its young lawmakers are playing reasoned and constructive roles in parliament. They are also presenting alternative policy frameworks.

However, the party is paying very little attention to engaging with citizens or connecting its reform agenda with their everyday needs. It is trying to win an impossible battle without first mobilising the public.

Moreover, the NCP appears to be facing a clear ‘Hamletian dilemma’. It finds itself caught between its stated commitment to pluralism, individual freedom and equal rights for all citizens on the one hand, and political pressure to appease conservative majority sentiment on the other.

Although the party publicly pledges to protect women's rights and Bangladesh's diverse cultural heritage, it often fails to stand firm on its policy positions and quickly opts for compromise. Like Shakespeare's Hamlet, the NCP moves towards taking a principled position but becomes hesitant when political courage is required to defend it. Its alliance with Jamaat has also undermined its credibility regarding its commitment to building an inclusive society.

The NCP suffers from another problem as well. Some of its leaders have not only embraced populist rhetoric but have also become involved in the kind of mudslinging politics characterised by personal insults, derogatory name-calling and the spread of conspiracy theories.

Although some NCP leaders have refused to take responsibility for this conduct by their colleagues, the party has yet to take any formal action against those involved. Such politics deepens divisions in society and creates a harmful ‘us versus them’ mentality. This is deeply concerning for the democratic future of Bangladesh.

As for other political forces outside parliament, left-wing parties suffer from a severe lack of organisational capacity; the ideology of far-right parties is fundamentally incompatible with liberal democracy; and although emerging youth-led political platforms demonstrate good intentions and embrace modern values, they still have a long way to go before establishing themselves as viable political forces.

The true strength of an opposition party in a country does not depend solely on its ability to bring down a government or its chances of winning an election. It is measured by its commitment to building institutions, expanding citizen participation and having the moral courage to defend the truth and protect the rights of others, even when doing so is unpopular.

Bangladesh needs an opposition politics that rises above the struggle for power and guarantees accountability, good governance and the establishment of a tolerant society. Without such an opposition, ‘democracy’ will remain nothing more than a ritual performed on election day, while the dream of genuine democratic governance will remain elusive.

item.title: China prefers to maintain relations with all political parties, whether in govt or in opposition: Liu Haixing
item.description:
Liu Haixing, minister of the International Department of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, has said China prefers to maintain relations with all political parties, whether in govt or in opposition.

"Where history illuminates the future, we see clearly that party-to-party exchanges play important roles in the development of our bilateral relations. We do not draw ideological lines, nor distinguish friends based on whether a party is in or out of government," he said in a written statement.

Liu Haixing has made the remarks at the "Where History Illuminates the Future: China-Bangladesh “Political Parties Plus” Roundtable & Inauguration Ceremony of the Bangladesh-China Centre for Party and State Governance Studies."

The Chinese leader said, "It gives me great pleasure to attend this roundtable. Listening to all our friends’ sharing just now has deeply touched me. Among you are witnesses to the establishment of China-Bangladesh diplomatic relations, participants in China-Bangladesh cooperation, and contributors to the friendship between our two countries."

"Through friendly exchanges with all major Bangladeshi political parties, we have added impetus to bilateral cooperation. Through in-depth exchanges and mutual learning, we have provided useful references for each other’s development," Liu Haixing added.

He also said, "Through forging links and pooling efforts for people’s well-being, we have consolidated the popular support for China-Bangladesh friendship through “political party plus” channels. History has bestowed on us a precious friendship that spans generations."

"Standing at a new historical starting point, we stand ready to work together with all sectors of society in Bangladesh to carry forward our friendship, foster consensus, deepen exchanges and mutual learning, and enhance people-to-people ties, so as to turn our traditional friendship into momentum for progress and let China-Bangladesh relations shine more brilliantly in the new era," the Chinese minister hoped.

Liu Haixing said, "What you have shared, steeped in the years gone by and rich with genuine emotion, fully impressed upon me that mutual understanding and affinity have always been the defining feature of China-Bangladesh relations, mutually beneficial cooperation has always been the mainstay of China-Bangladesh engagement, and joint development has always been the shared aspiration of the peoples of China and Bangladesh."

"I cherish a special bond with Bangladesh. Forty-six years ago, my father served as China’s Ambassador to Bangladesh. From then on, I often heard him speak of the hardworking and kind-hearted Bangladeshi people and his deep affection for this land caressed by monsoon. This reflects the continuity of China-Bangladesh friendship, and reinforces my conviction that our friendship enjoys enduring vitality that transcends time, takes deep root among our peoples, and grows ever stronger," he added.

The Chinese Communist Party leader said, "China and Bangladesh are linked by mountains and seas. Across the millennia, we have respected each other amid exchanges of civilizations, stood by one another amid shifting circumstances, and advanced side by side along our development journeys, jointly writing a remarkable chapter of friendship between close neighbours."

"The theme of our exchange today is Where History Illuminates the Future. History not only records our precious past, but also lights the path ahead," he believed.

Liu Haixing mentioned, "Ten years ago, General Secretary Xi Jinping paid a historic visit to Bangladesh, elevating bilateral relations to a strategic cooperative partnership. Last June, General Secretary Xi Jinping met with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman during his visit to China. The two leaders jointly announced the building of a China-Bangladesh community with a shared future in the new era, charting the course for a new chapter in our friendship."

"We must stay firmly on course and jointly build a path of trust. Since the establishment of diplomatic relations, China and Bangladesh have been committed to friendship. We stand firm as trusted good friends, neighbours and partners. Amid profound changes unseen in a century, it is all the more important for us to follow the guidance of our leaders, and firmly respect, understand and support one another on issues bearing on each other’s core interests and major concerns," he said.

The Chinese leader said, "We must light the way for each other and jointly build a path of development. Over the past five decades, bilateral trade surged from 15 million to more than 23 billion US dollars. Bangladesh was the first South Asian country to sign a memorandum of understanding on Belt and Road cooperation with China."

"Over the years, a host of projects including highways, bridges and tunnels have been delivered across Bangladesh, giving a strong boost to local economic and social development. Today, progress is steady on major projects such as the Mongla Port Industrial Park and the comprehensive treatment and restoration of the Teesta River. We believe these initiatives will bring greater benefits to peoples of both countries. We must stand together through thick and thin and jointly build a path of friendship," Liu Haixing said.

He said, "In ancient times, Xuanzang traveled westward in search of Buddhist scriptures and Atisha came to China to spread the Dharma, forging a millennia-old bond between us. Today, nine China-Bangladesh Friendship Bridges bear witness to new chapters of our friendship."

"During this visit, I will attend Lighting Up the Future: “Political Parties Plus” People-to-People Cooperation Programme, bringing smart classrooms and stationery to a school in Dhaka. I hope such “small yet beautiful” projects can not only light up the future of children, but also help pass on and nourish China-Bangladesh friendship," the Chinese leader added.

Liu Haixing said, "We must pool our strength and jointly build a path of collaboration. We meet at a time when changes unseen in a century are accelerating across the world and the international order is undergoing its most profound transformation since the end of the Cold War. We should work together to act on the four Global Initiatives put forward by General Secretary Xi Jinping, step up communication and coordination within multilateral frameworks including the UN, and promote an equal and orderly multipolar world and a universally beneficial and inclusive economic globalization. This will better safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of China, Bangladesh and the shared interests of the Global South."

"China-Bangladesh friendship is not an undertaking of a small number of people, but a consensus across all sectors of our societies. That is what makes it so precious. Polls show that 90 percent of Bangladeshi people hold a favorable opinion of China. This hard-won achievement deserves to be cherished," he added.

The Chinese minister said, "Friends present here today come from different sectors, including political parties, the government, businesses, think tanks, media and social organizations. Over the years, you have devoted yourselves to your respective fields and helped nurture the foundation of China-Bangladesh friendship with great care. We count on your continuous efforts to further consolidate the broad consensus for friendship between our two countries, and let the tree of China-Bangladesh friendship flourish ever more vibrantly."

"At present, both countries are at key development junctures. China has begun the implementation of the 15th Five-Year Plan, while Bangladesh has entered a new stage of political transition. As political parties in our respective countries shoulder important responsibilities, it is highly timely to strengthen exchanges of governance experience. Today, we are pleased to see the inauguration of the Bangladesh-China Centre for Party and State Governance Studies. This is a tangible step to implement the important consensus reached between our two leaders, which also responds to the practical needs of both sides and the shared expectations of our peoples," he said.

Liu Haixing believed, "Going forward, it is hoped that the Centre will deepen research on and interpretation of the underlying logic of governance of the two countries to enhance mutual understanding; share each other’s governance philosophies to enhance mutual learning; and boost cooperation across the board to deepen China-Bangladesh friendship. We hope that the Centre can facilitate more exchanges between political parties, youths, business communities, media outlets and think tanks, so as to contribute to building a China-Bangladesh community with a shared future in the new era."

"This year marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the Communist Party of China. As a century-old major party still in its prime, the CPC has been continuously exploring ways to strengthen itself. Since the 18th CPC National Congress, centering on the epochal question of what kind of long-term ruling Marxist political party we should build and how to build it, the CPC Central Committee with Comrade Xi Jinping at its core has put forward a series of new ideas, thinking and strategies to govern, invigorate and strengthen the Party, thus forming Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building," the Chinese leader added.

"Last week, the CPC successfully convened the Fifth Plenary Session of the 20th CPC Central Committee, during which important arrangements were made for Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance from the strategic height of consolidating the ruling status of the Party and fulfilling its missions and tasks. We are ready to strengthen exchanges on the outcome of the Plenary Session, especially Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building with political parties and all sectors of Bangladesh," he added.

item.title: Democrats take US Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump
item.description:
USA-ELECTION/TEXAS

Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump.

Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Trump's stewardship of the country.

In Texas, the biggest Republican state, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning a Senate seat and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott.

Abdul El-Sayed becomes first Muslim elected to US Senate

Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate.

The results will usher in a new era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in Trump.

Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump's administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump's nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.

"There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America," said Chuck Schumer, the party's Senate minority leader. "Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must deliver."

Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, has exercised an iron grip on his party for most of the last decade. But the new balance of power in Washington may accelerate his lame-duck status, as attention turns toward the 2028 presidential race and potential successors begin competing for political influence in a post-Trump world.

Despite worries from Democrats that Trump might seek to overturn the election results, as he did in 2020, the president accepted the outcome, congratulating Democrats in an interview with Fox News. He also said he would work with Democrats on issues such as immigration, though he threatened to veto any "insane" bills they passed.

Democratic wave

Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump's tariff policy and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House.

Republicans, led by Trump, attacked Democrats over culture war issues such as transgender rights while portraying their opponents as radical and extreme. But in poll after poll, voters made it clear they were far more concerned with pocketbook issues.

The Democratic wave flooded huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in all but a handful of the approximately 2,100 counties where most votes had been counted, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today.

Democrats made gains in the richest counties and the poorest; in counties where more people have college degrees and where fewer do. Democrats' advances were particularly sharp in heavily Latino counties, including the border counties of Texas that shifted toward Trump in 2024 and the agricultural towns of the Kansas prairie.

In Seward County, Kansas, home to one of America's biggest beef processing plants and where about half of eligible voters are Hispanic, Democrat Adam Hamilton led incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 13 points, two years after Trump won the county by 39 points.

Democrats flipped more than two dozen House seats currently held by Republicans, locking in a majority. Democrats won all the closely contested House races that have been decided so far, and they won about a dozen races in districts that Trump won by double digits two years ago.

An unprecedented Republican gambit to redraw several House districts to make them more favorable largely failed, with Democrats hanging on to most of the targeted seats.

Midterm elections are typically seen as a referendum on the sitting president, and Trump did little to disabuse voters of that notion. In the campaign's final weeks, he held dozens of rallies, telling supporters repeatedly to "pretend I'm on the ballot."

He also intervened in several Republican primaries earlier this year to ensure his preferred candidates reached the ballot, despite concerns from some Republicans that his choices carried significant liabilities.

In Texas, Trump backed Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden state attorney general, over the incumbent, Senator John Cornyn. In South Carolina, the president anointed Darline Graham, a political neophyte, after her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly earlier this year. Both candidates lost.

But even candidates who sought to distance themselves from Trump were unable to escape voters' wrath. In Maine, Republican incumbent Susan Collins had her 30-year Senate career end on Tuesday, despite emphasizing her willingness to break with the president during the campaign.

Progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan’s open Senate seat, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber. He defeated Mike Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent, who entered the race with Trump's backing and sought to falsely portray El-Sayed, an Egyptian American born in Michigan, as a religious extremist.

"You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope," El-Sayed told cheering supporters on Tuesday night, referring to Rogers.

Competitive Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska had yet to be called early on Wednesday.

On Tuesday night, as it grew clear Republicans were in danger of losing their congressional majorities, Trump wrote on social media, "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"

In media interviews, Trump acknowledged the conflict with Iran had played a role in his party's losses but stood by his decision to go to war.

Voters rebuke Trump

According to exit polls conducted by SSRS on behalf of a consortium of US media outlets including major television networks and the Associated Press, half of voters nationwide said they saw the 2026 midterm elections as an opportunity to rebuke the president, and three-quarters said they are "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the way the country is headed.

In addition, 70 per cent of voters surveyed said they want Congress to provide more checks and balances on the president.

"In sweeping and decisive victories, the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the man named President Donald J. Trump," incumbent Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia told supporters at a victory party.

The night included several historic firsts for both parties. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state, while Byron Donalds won Florida's gubernatorial race to become the first Black Republican governor in the US. Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, while Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California's first Latino governor.

item.title: Arrest warrant issued against actress Pori Moni
item.description:
A court has issued an arrest warrant against actress Pori Moni in an attempted murder case filed by businessman Nasir Uddin Mahmud.

Senior Judicial Magistrate of Dhaka Mahfuzur Rahman passed the order today, Wednesday (4 November).

Pori Moni's lawyer, Nilanjana Suravi, confirmed the development to Prothom Alo.

She said Pori Moni could not appear before the court today due to an allergy-related illness. Her lawyer had filed a petition seeking an adjournment and a new date for the next hearing. However, the court rejected the petition and ordered an arrest warrant against her client.

Court sources said the plaintiff in the case appeared before the court today and sought cancellation of the accused persons' bail. No lawyer representing the accused was present at the hearing. Following the hearing, the court cancelled their bail and ordered the issuance of arrest warrants.

According to court sources, Pori Moni's lawyer, Nilanjana, stated in the petition for an adjournment that the case was scheduled for recording witness testimony today. However, the accused, Pori Moni, was unable to appear in court due to an allergy-related illness, making an adjournment necessary. Otherwise, she would suffer irreparable loss, the petition said.

Nasir Uddin filed the case with a Dhaka court on 6 July 2022. According to the complaint, Pori Moni and her associates consume alcohol and visit various prestigious clubs when they get the opportunity. They drink alcohol and take away bottles without paying for them. The complaint also alleged that Pori Moni threatened to harass people by filing false cases through police officers known to her.

The complaint stated that shortly after midnight on 9 June 2021, the accused entered the Savar Boat Club and used a washroom on the second floor.

They later sat inside the club and consumed alcohol. At around 1:15am, when the plaintiff and his associate Shah Shahidul Alam were leaving the club, Pori Moni allegedly called Nasir Uddin and asked him to sit with them for a while.

At one point, Pori Moni allegedly tried to attract Nasir Uddin through obscene gestures and pressured him to give her a bottle of Blue Label whisky free of charge. When he refused, she allegedly abused him verbally.

During an argument between the plaintiff and the accused, Pori Moni allegedly threw a serving glass at Nasir Uddin and also hurled her mobile phone at him. As a result, Nasir Uddin sustained injuries to his head and chest. The complaint further alleged that Pori Moni and her associates assaulted him, threatened to kill him and vandalised property.

On 18 March 2024, investigation officer Mohammad Monir Hossain, an inspector with the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), Dhaka district, submitted a report to the Chief Judicial Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, stating that the allegations of assault and intimidation against Pori Moni and her costume designer, Junaid Baghdadi Jimmy, also known as Jim, had been substantiated.

However, the investigation found no evidence supporting the allegations against another accused, Fatema Tuz Jannat Boni. On 26 January last year, the same court framed charges against the two accused and ordered the commencement of their trial.

Meanwhile, over the same incident, Pori Moni filed a case with Savar Police Station against the plaintiff and another person, accusing them of attempted rape and murder. The case is currently pending before Dhaka's Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal No. 9.
