item.title: Workers' protest: Additional police, water cannons deployed in Mirpur, Uttara
item.description:
Police have deployed additional personnel in the capital’s Mirpur and Uttara areas as garment workers continue protests demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
In Pallabi, police dispersed workers who had gathered in front of several garment factories, while law enforcement agencies remained on high alert in Uttara.
The heightened security measures have been in place since Wednesday morning.
Md Hafizur Rahman, officer-in-charge of Mirpur Model Police Station, said there had been no major incidents related to the workers’ protests in the area.
Of the eight garment factories under the police station’s jurisdiction, seven remained operational. Workers at one factory had initially stopped working but resumed operations after being persuaded to do so, he said.
Additional police personnel had been deployed since the morning and remained on high alert, the OC added.
Earlier on Wednesday, police dispersed workers who had gathered outside several garment factories in an alley near Purabi Cinema Hall in Mirpur-11. Tension arose between workers and police, but no untoward incidents were reported.
In Uttara, police and other law enforcement personnel were also on high alert. Police took positions along the stretch from Rajlokkhi to the airport to prevent any untoward incidents. Water cannons and police vans were stationed in the area.
On November 1, garment workers blocked roads in Mirpur, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. Clashes and chases between workers and police continued from morning until afternoon. At one point, a police vehicle was set on fire beneath the Mirpur-11 metro rail station.
Police have since detained several people from different parts of Mirpur on suspicion of involvement in the incidents.
Garment workers also staged protests in Mirpur on Monday and Tuesday. Workers in Gazipur, Savar, Ashulia and Narayanganj have also been demonstrating over the wage demand. The protests have led to clashes, disrupted production at several factories and forced some to suspend operations.
Taufiq Sheikh, a garment worker injured during the protests in Gazipur, died on Tuesday afternoon while undergoing treatment at Shin-Shin Japan Hospital in Uttara, Dhaka.

item.title: SAU students block roads again in Agargaon over research field
item.description:
More than 1,000 students of Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University (SAU) blocked roads in Agargaon on Wednesday, demanding the restoration of their former research field.
Around 11am, the students marched from the university's flagpole area and took positions at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Centre intersection, bringing traffic to a halt.
The protesters also announced plans to burn an effigy in front of the Public Works Department (PWD) complex in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar on Wednesday.
At a meeting between teachers and students on Tuesday, the protesters announced a boycott of all examinations and said they would not attend classes scheduled after 11am.
Later that night, around 10pm, students from all academic batches gathered at the university's TSC premises and declared an indefinite shutdown. As a result, all academic activities were suspended from Wednesday.
The protests began on October 27, with students claiming that the former trade fair grounds belonged to the university and demanding that the land be handed over to it.
On that day, students seized machinery and vehicles being used for soil testing ahead of the planned construction of a secretariat building on the site and brought them onto the campus.
The following day, after issuing an ultimatum to halt fair-related activities, students vandalised several structures on the grounds.
On October 29, they blocked roads. That same day, State Minister for Youth and Sports Md Aminul Haque announced the suspension of all fairs, including the National Youth Fair.
However, the protesters continued their agitation, demanding the removal of structures from the site and withdrawal of cases filed against unidentified students.
On November 2, they took further action by tilling the land and asserting control over it.

item.title: Hospital vandalized in Mohammadpur over medical bill discount dispute
item.description:
City Hospital and Diagnostic Centre in the capital’s Mohammadpur area was vandalized by a group of young men following a dispute over a discount on a patient's medical bill.
Several people have been arrested in connection with a case filed over the incident, and police are verifying their involvement.
The attack took place around midnight on Tuesday when a group of young men entered the hospital and vandalized the premises. The front section of the facility and its ground-floor reception area were damaged, with furniture and medical equipment left in disarray.
According to hospital sources, a patient named Asma had received treatment at the facility for a lip injury. Her medical bill amounted to Tk2,780, and her relatives requested a discount.
Hospital authorities agreed to reduce the bill partially, but an argument followed. After the patient received treatment and left, a group of young men gathered at the hospital and carried out the attack.
Mohammad Usman Gani, assistant manager of City Hospital Ltd, said the attackers had arrived from the direction of the Graphic Arts Institute.
He alleged that the attackers also looted the facility, causing an estimated Tk50-60 lakh in losses.
Police said they were reviewing CCTV footage to identify those involved. Hospital authorities have filed a case over the incident.
Abdul Halim, officer-in-charge of Mohammadpur police station, confirmed that several people had been arrested in connection with the case. Their involvement is being further investigated, he said.

item.title: Garment worker injured in Gazipur unrest dies in hospital
item.description:
Garment worker Toufiq Sheikh, 22, who was injured during unrest in Gazipur, died at a hospital in Dhaka on Tuesday.
He was a junior layman in the cutting section of Laila Styles Ltd.
Toufiq died at Shin Shin Japan Hospital in Uttara, where he had been undergoing treatment. His body reached his village in Chhaygharia, Gobindaganj, Gaibandha, at around 10pm.
His janaza was scheduled for 9:30am on Wednesday, followed by burial at the village graveyard.
According to his family, Toufiq was recording the unrest on his mobile phone on Monday when he was attacked and beaten.
However, police official Mohammad Belayet Hossain gave a different account, saying outsiders had pressured the factory to shut down, triggering a clash with workers.
Toufiq's brother, Harun Mia, and local teacher Pradip Kumar also spoke about the incident. Officer-in-Charge Mahfuz Alam, Union Parishad chairman Zahurul Haque and Toufiq's uncle Bachchu Mia were among those who provided information about the incident.

item.title: Police fire tear gas as workers throw bricks on Dhaka-Mymensingh highway
item.description:
Police fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse garment workers after they threw bricks and stones at law enforcement personnel on the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway near the Signboard area under Gazipur’s Gacha police station on Wednesday morning.
Traffic came to a standstill around 9:30am after workers occupied the highway, bringing vehicles to a halt.
Mohammad Amjad Hossain, superintendent of the Gazipur Industrial Police, said the situation had been calm earlier in the morning.
Around 9:30am, between 2,000 and 4,000 workers took to the streets in the Gacha police station area. A standoff followed, with workers throwing bricks and stones at police, prompting law enforcement personnel to fire tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse them, he said.
Earlier, around 8:30am, another group of workers had gathered near Joydebpur but was also dispersed.
Amjad said the situation remained stable in Salna, Rajendrapur, Shafipur and Palli Bidyut, while tension persisted near Kashimpur. Police remained on high alert, he added.

item.title: Ishraque Hossain named president of martial arts confederation
item.description:
Dhaka-6 MP Ishraque Hossain has been appointed president of the new ad-hoc committee of the Bangladesh Martial Arts Confederation.
Former athlete and sports organizer Mahfuz Hasan has been named its general secretary.
The 29-member committee was announced on Tuesday through an order signed by Md Doltuzzaman Khan, executive director of the National Sports Council (NSC).
According to the order, the previous ad-hoc committee has been dissolved and replaced by the new body, which has been tasked with holding an election within the next three months and handing over responsibility to the elected committee.
The committee has six vice-presidents: Jasmine Nahar, secretary at the Ministry of Primary and Mass Education; Md Monirul Islam, an athlete and sports organizer; Engineer Md Abdul Halim, CEO of Mallick Group; sports organizer Mohammad Tarikul Alam; Md Shahidul Islam; and Shahed Wahed Ali.
Md Shahadat Hossain Khan and Sayeed Md Alvi have been appointed joint secretaries, while Md Habibullah Parvez has been named treasurer.
The committee also includes sports organizers, former athletes, coaches, and international referees and judges.
The NSC said the committee was formed to arrange an election in accordance with the constitution of the Bangladesh Martial Arts Confederation and transfer responsibility to the elected body within three months.

item.title: Four killed in head-on collision between bus, laguna in Mirpur
item.description:
Four people, including two women, were killed in a head-on collision between an Asian University bus and a laguna in the Nawab-er-Bagh area of Diabari, Mirpur Beribadh, on Wednesday morning.
The accident occurred around 7:38am within the jurisdiction of Shah Ali police station, said Talha Bin Jasim, media officer of the Fire Service and Civil Defence.
A unit from Kalyanpur Fire Station rushed to the scene after receiving the report and began rescue operations.
According to the Fire Service, the collision took place around 7:30am on Nawab-er-Bagh Road when a speeding passenger bus hit the laguna coming from the opposite direction, killing four people — two men and two women.
No other injuries were reported.
Police arrived at the scene shortly after the accident and took steps to restore normal traffic movement.

item.title: 25 platoons of BGB, SRB, Ansar deployed in Gazipur amid worker unrest
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), the Special Reserve Battalion (SRB) and Ansar personnel have been deployed alongside police in Gazipur's industrial areas to maintain law and order amid ongoing garment worker protests over wage demands.
Md Arif Hossain, assistant commissioner (Media and Research Cell) at the Gazipur deputy commissioner's office, confirmed the deployment on Wednesday morning.
He said 10 BGB platoons and 21 executive magistrates were initially deployed on Monday. The deployment was increased on Tuesday to 11 BGB platoons and 25 executive magistrates.
On Wednesday, another BGB platoon was added, bringing the total to 12. Eight SRB platoons and five Ansar platoons were also deployed.
In total, 25 platoons of BGB, SRB and Ansar personnel are working to maintain law and order in Gazipur's industrial areas under the supervision of 25 executive magistrates, Arif said.
As of 8:30am on Wednesday, no reports of worker protests or highway blockades had been received from anywhere in Gazipur.
Traffic on the Dhaka-Tangail and Dhaka-Mymensingh highways was moving normally, he added.

item.title: Why Bangladesh is missing the technology revolution
item.description:
A country can become increasingly connected without becoming technologically advanced. It can expand internet access, digitize public services, produce thousands of computer science graduates, and encourage young people to pursue freelancing, yet remain a marginal player in the global technology economy.
Bangladesh risks becoming such a country. While the world is reorganizing its economic architecture around artificial intelligence, semiconductors, robotics, and advanced manufacturing, Bangladesh is still struggling to move beyond the consumption and adaptation of technologies developed elsewhere.
The uncomfortable question is whether the country is preparing to participate in the next industrial transformation or merely positioning itself as a market for its products. The distinction matters because the nature of economic competition is changing.
For decades, Bangladesh's comparative advantages have rested largely on inexpensive labour, export-oriented manufacturing, and a large domestic market. These advantages helped sustain growth, particularly through the ready-made garment industry.
But the emerging global economy increasingly rewards something different: The capacity to generate knowledge, develop intellectual property, design sophisticated products, and commercialize scientific discoveries. The countries that control these capabilities will exercise disproportionate influence over trade, investment, and the distribution of economic power.
The transformation is already visible in the corporate landscape. Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and TSMC represent more than successful businesses. They illustrate how technological capabilities can become strategic national assets.
South Korea's Samsung has been central to its industrial development, while Taiwan's semiconductor industry has established the country as an indispensable part of the global technology supply chain. These achievements were built through sustained investments in research, industrial expertise, and institutional capacity. Technology did not simply follow their economic progress; it helped create it.
The scale of the emerging opportunity is extraordinary. UNCTAD estimates that the global market for 17 frontier technologies, including artificial intelligence, the internet of things, and advanced robotics, could expand to $16.4 trillion by 2033. The AI market alone could approach $4.8 trillion.
Meanwhile, digitally delivered services have already become a multitrillion-dollar segment of international trade. This is not a distant technological possibility. It is an economic transformation unfolding in real time, attracting investment and reshaping the competitive relationship between nations.
Yet Bangladesh's participation remains remarkably modest. The country had set an ambitious target of earning $5bn from ICT exports by 2025. Actual ICT service exports amounted to approximately $724.6m in the 2024-25 fiscal year.
The shortfall is revealing. India has developed an enormous international technology services industry, while Pakistan's reported technology services exports have also exceeded Bangladesh's. The issue is not simply the difference in export earnings. It is the difference in the industrial ecosystems, research capabilities, and international market presence that make such earnings possible.
Bangladesh's predicament is perhaps best understood as an innovation trap - it has made progress in adopting digital technologies but has not developed a corresponding capacity to produce them. It has expanded the number of technology users without building enough technology creators.
Providing services through existing platforms is economically useful; designing the platforms, developing the underlying technologies, and owning the intellectual property can generate substantially greater strategic value.
The roots of this problem extend deep into the education system. Bangladesh continues to measure educational achievement primarily through examinations, grades, and certificates. Students are trained to reproduce information more efficiently than to challenge it, experiment with it, or transform it into new knowledge.
This approach may produce academic credentials, but technological innovation demands a different intellectual culture. It requires curiosity, independent reasoning, tolerance for failure, and the ability to connect knowledge across disciplines. These qualities cannot flourish in an environment where completing the syllabus often takes precedence over developing the capacity to think.
The answer, however, is not to dismiss humanities and social sciences in favour of engineering and computer science. Technological development is not exclusively a scientific enterprise.
Artificial intelligence raises questions of ethics, language, law, culture, and social responsibility. Advanced manufacturing requires management, communication, and institutional expertise.
What Bangladesh needs is an education system capable of connecting scientific knowledge with social understanding and practical application. The problem is not the presence of particular academic disciplines but the absence of meaningful intellectual and professional integration among them.
The weakness of the research environment makes this educational limitation even more serious. According to the University Grants Commission, public universities allocated only Tk190.65 crore for research out of a total approved budget of approximately Tk13,222 crore in the 2025-26 fiscal year. That amounts to around 1.44%.
Even this modest allocation is not always fully utilized. How can universities become centres of innovation when research remains a marginal component of their institutional priorities?
A university should be more than an institution that supplies graduates to the employment market. It should be a place where existing knowledge is questioned, new ideas are developed, and practical solutions emerge.
In Bangladesh, however, the connection between academic research and economic production remains weak. Researchers frequently lack adequate laboratories, funding, technological equipment, and opportunities to work with industries. Businesses, meanwhile, often prefer imported solutions because domestic research institutions cannot consistently provide commercially viable alternatives.
This disconnect creates a peculiar economic contradiction. Universities produce graduates, industries complain about the shortage of appropriately skilled workers, and the government invests in technology-related infrastructure, yet these three components rarely operate as parts of a coherent system. The result is an economy in which academic knowledge struggles to become industrial capability.
Memoranda of understanding and occasional research collaborations cannot resolve this structural problem. What is required is a permanent framework for industry-funded research, university-based innovation centres, technology incubation, and the commercialization of locally developed intellectual property.
The semiconductor sector offers a glimpse of what Bangladesh might achieve, provided its ambitions are matched by institutional preparation. According to BIDA, the country has more than 700 chip designers and recorded semiconductor-related exports exceeding $8m in 2024.
The ambition to increase exports to $1bn by 2030 is significant. But semiconductor development is not simply a matter of producing more designers. It involves specialized infrastructure, advanced research, substantial investment, intellectual property protection, and integration into complex international supply chains.
Bangladesh must recognize the distance between having a small presence in chip design and becoming a meaningful participant in the global semiconductor industry.
Artificial intelligence presents a similar challenge. Developing a Bengali-language large language model may be strategically important, particularly for a country with a large linguistic community. But a national AI ambition cannot be reduced to developing a model or announcing a policy.
It requires reliable datasets, computing capacity, skilled researchers, cybersecurity safeguards and an ecosystem capable of translating applications into productive services. Without these foundations, technological ambitions risk becoming another collection of policy documents with limited practical consequences.
There is also a governance dimension that deserves greater attention. Technological investment depends on confidence in institutions. Investors need predictable regulations, transparent decision-making, effective protection of intellectual property, and a stable policy environment.
Bureaucratic complications and frequent policy changes can undermine long-term investment, particularly in industries where research and product development require years before generating returns.
Public expenditure must also be judged by what it produces. Spending on buildings, equipment, and digital infrastructure is not synonymous with technological progress if these investments do not strengthen research, productivity, and innovation.
The objective should not be to accumulate technology projects, distribute devices, or increase the number of digital services. It should be to develop an economy capable of creating technological solutions to its own problems and competing in international markets.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.

item.title: Low-income children’s schooling at risk as education costs rise
item.description:
Although students in government primary and secondary schools receive free textbooks, parents are spending thousands of taka each year to keep their children in education.
Costs for private tuition, coaching, guidebooks, notebooks, stationery, uniforms, shoes, transport and examination fees are placing an increasing burden on households, particularly those with low or limited incomes.
For some families, financial hardship has forced them to send their children to residential madrasas, while others have withdrawn their children from school and put them to work.
The Education Watch 2023 study on education monitoring, conducted by the Campaign for Popular Education (CAMPE), provides an overview of household spending on students.
According to the study, the average annual household expenditure on a primary school student was Tk13,882 in 2022, compared with Tk27,340 for a secondary school student. This means families spent almost twice as much on a secondary-level student as on a primary-level one.
The costs were higher in urban areas. In 2022, the average annual household expenditure per primary student in cities stood at Tk18,132, while the figure for secondary students was Tk35,662.
The study also found a sharp rise in spending during the first six months of 2023. During that period, households spent Tk8,647 on average per primary student and Tk20,712 per secondary student.
Based on the expenditure recorded in the first half of 2023 compared with the 2022 figures, researchers estimated that annual education costs had risen by 25% at the primary level and 51% at the secondary level.
These figures, however, are several years old. Since then, the cost of living—including prices of essential goods, house rents and transport—has continued to rise.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), overall inflation stood at 8.34% in September 2026, while wage growth was 7.9%. Wage growth has remained below inflation for 56 consecutive months, reducing the real purchasing power of people on limited incomes and making it increasingly difficult for families to meet education expenses.
Marjina Khatun, 45, from Uluhati village in Nandail Upazila of Mymensingh, lives in a rented home on Road 2 behind Nabodoy Bazar in Dhaka’s Mohammadpur.
As her husband’s income is insufficient to support the family, she works as a domestic worker in three households, earning around Tk9,000 a month. Her husband, Moti Mia, drives a battery-powered rickshaw in the capital. After paying the daily rental charge and garage fees, he takes home Tk500-600 a day. Even then, the couple has to borrow money to meet household expenses.
Of their three children, their eldest daughter, Sadia Akter Mohona, is married. Marjina said she could not continue her daughter’s education because of financial constraints.
Their second daughter, Samia Akter, is in Class VII at Sandipan School in the Nabodoy area, while their youngest daughter, Lamia Akter, is in kindergarten.
Marjina said Samia’s monthly tuition fee is Tk700. Although she received free textbooks for Class VII, the family had to spend Tk1,500 on guidebooks and Tk550 on notebooks and pens. They also have to pay for her school uniform, shoes and bag.
In total, the family spends around Tk11,000-12,000 a year on Samia’s education, she said.
Moti Mia said his earnings from driving a rickshaw used to be higher, while the rental charge was lower. His income has now fallen by nearly half, making it impossible to cover household expenses and his daughters’ education costs. As a result, his wife has also had to work in other people’s homes.
Meanwhile, a parent in Mirpur provided a breakdown of the expenses for a child studying at Cantonment Public School, estimating the first-year cost at around Tk238,200.
The admission fee is Tk22,000. Books, notebooks and stationery cost Tk5,000, while the uniform costs Tk2,200, shoes Tk1,000 and a schoolbag Tk3,000. The family also spends Tk2,000 on guidebooks and another Tk3,000 on optional books. An additional Tk2,000 is required annually for class parties, picnics and educational trips.
The parent, who requested anonymity, said the monthly expenses include Tk5,000 in tuition fees, Tk7,000 for the school bus, Tk1,500 for notebooks and pens, and around Tk3,000 for tiffin.
This brings the monthly expenditure to Tk16,500, or Tk198,000 a year. In addition, the school charges Tk700 for each examination, while students are fined Tk50 for every day they are absent.
The parent said the family could not afford a school with even higher fees, which was why they chose Cantonment Public School.
Some parents who cannot afford the expenses of mainstream schools are turning to alternative institutions.
Delwar Hossain, a rickshaw driver living in Mohammadpur Housing Society, said he had admitted his child to a residential madrasa because he could not afford the cost of regular schooling. The monthly fee of Tk1,500 covers accommodation and meals.
Rasel, a rickshaw driver living in Dhaka Udyan, has three sons. Unable to bear the cost of their education, he sent his eldest son, 15-year-old Niloy, to work at a garment factory. His second son, 10-year-old Nirob, has also been taken out of school and put to work at a chicken shop.
His youngest son, eight-year-old Nehat, attends Protiva School near their home, where the monthly fee is Tk1,500. Rasel said even this expense had become difficult to manage and that he was considering enrolling the boy in a government primary school.
Education researcher KM Enamul Haque said household spending on primary and secondary education had increased since the 2022 study, as living costs had risen while people's incomes had not kept pace.
The burden was particularly severe for families from marginalised communities, he said.
He added that financial hardship was forcing many children from disadvantaged backgrounds to enter the workforce and abandon their studies.
To address the situation, investment in education must increase, inequalities must be reduced and measures must be taken to keep children in school, he said.
Haque also noted that families could spend less by sending their children to government primary schools, which are more widely available. However, dissatisfaction among parents over the quality of education at these institutions has contributed to the growth of kindergarten schools in both urban and rural areas, increasing household expenses.
He stressed the need to improve the quality of government primary schools.
Educationist, children's author, education columnist and former principal Md Rahmat Ullah said disparities in access to public and private education were also contributing to rising costs.
Although government primary schools are widely available, many parents turn to private institutions because they are dissatisfied with the quality of education, he said. At the secondary level, private schools outnumber government institutions, leaving many students with little choice but to attend fee-charging schools.
Alongside school fees, families also have to spend substantial amounts on private tuition, he added.
Rahmat Ullah called for an expansion of government primary schools and improvements in their teaching standards, as well as the establishment of more government secondary schools.
He also stressed the need to improve benefits for teachers at private institutions to attract qualified professionals to the sector. Ensuring effective working hours for teachers and reducing disparities across different streams of education were also essential, he said.
The government must take responsibility for ensuring quality education for all, he added.
Alongside free textbooks, the government has taken an initiative to provide students at government primary schools with free uniforms, shoes and jute bags.
The Ministry of Primary and Mass Education said the programme was being implemented under the directive of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. Education Minister Dr ANM Ehsanul Hoque Milon had earlier announced that the initiative would begin on a pilot basis in July.
Under the first phase, the government planned to distribute the items among around 100,000 Class I students at 3,522 government primary schools across 25 upazilas and thanas.
However, distribution had not begun at schools even by early November.
As of September 20, the Directorate of Primary Education had received 205,000 sets of uniforms, 67,900 pairs of shoes and 115,216 bags.
Once distributed, the items are expected to reduce some of the expenses parents of primary school students face for uniforms, shoes and bags.
Professor Dr Abdullah Al-Mamun, a member of the University Grants Commission (UGC), said investment in education must not be reduced despite rising expenditure on students.
The government was providing various forms of support to students and had also taken an initiative to distribute uniforms, shoes and bags to schoolchildren. Even so, education costs continued to rise, he said.
He told Bangla Tribune that such spending should be viewed as an investment in developing the country's human resources.
“We are now enjoying the benefits of the demographic dividend. It is essential to make use of this period to develop human resources. The government is trying to rebuild the economy amid various challenges. Even in this situation, steps have been taken to increase allocations for education. The target is to raise education spending to 5% of GDP. The allocation for the sector has already been increased to 2%,” he said.
He added, “Spending on education is never a bad investment. The positive impact of investment in education is recognised around the world. Education plays an important role in creating employment and developing skills. Therefore, expenditure on education should not be viewed simply as a cost, but as an investment in building human resources.”

item.title: Sajek grinds to halt as 14-day blockade triggers food shortages
item.description:
Sajek in Rangamati has remained cut off for 14 consecutive days as a road blockade continued on Wednesday, disrupting the supply of essential goods and leaving people facing an increasingly severe food shortage.
The blockade has also left farmers struggling to transport their produce to markets, while hundreds of drivers and their assistants who depend on tourist transport services are being forced to run their households on borrowed money. Many vehicle owners are also worried about repaying loan instalments.
Adding to the uncertainty, the Sajek Gono Odhikar Rakkha Committee has announced a 48-hour blockade on Wednesday and Thursday in protest against the ongoing blockade in Sajek. The programme was announced in a press release signed by the organisation’s member secretary, Bindu Lal Chakma, on Tuesday evening.
The latest announcement has further stalled efforts to bring the administration and protesters to the negotiating table. Although progress had been made towards resolving four of the five demands, no agreement has been reached on the central point of disagreement. As a result, the indefinite road blockade remains in place.
With another round of blockade underway, Sajek’s tourism, transport, trade and local economy are facing severe disruption. Leaders of the two organisations leading the movement have, however, announced some exemptions for the transport of agricultural produce and vehicles carrying teachers and students.
In a joint statement to the media on Tuesday, Sajek Gono Odhikar Rakkha Committee convener Babudhan Chakma and Sajek Karbari Association President Natun Joy Chakma said the decision had been taken at a joint meeting of the two organisations.
They said vehicles transporting locally produced agricultural goods, as well as those carrying teachers and students to schools, colleges and universities, would be exempted from the blockade.
The exemptions would be added to those already announced for emergency services, including ambulances, electricity supply vehicles, vehicles used for religious and wedding ceremonies, and those carrying journalists.
The decision was taken in consideration of the interests of farmers and agricultural traders from both indigenous and Bengali communities in Sajek, they said. However, the indefinite blockade would continue until all five demands of Sajek residents were met.
The Sajek Gono Odhikar Rakkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association resumed the blockade on Monday after a one-day relaxation on Sunday. On Tuesday, vehicle movement remained virtually suspended after protesters placed tree trunks and lit fires at several points along the Sajek tourist road.
At a meeting between protesters and a government delegation at Ujopara Bazar on October 26, the two sides reportedly reached an understanding on four of the five demands. However, discussions failed to produce a final decision because of disagreement over the demand to remove armed members of the Parbatya Chattagram Jana Samhati Samiti from Sajek.
Although another round of talks was promised, no effective initiative for a fresh meeting has been reported. Protesters have said the blockade will continue until all their demands are met.
Baghaichari Upazila Nirbahi Officer Amena Marjan said no decision had yet been made about holding another meeting. She added that, following instructions from the district administration and in view of security concerns, Sajek Valley tourist destination would remain closed until further notice.
On November 1, protesters had announced a 12-hour relaxation of the blockade to allow residents to collect food and essential supplies. However, a counter-blockade by the Parbatya Chattagram Rakkha Committee and a work stoppage by transport owners and workers prevented normal traffic from resuming that day. Local residents said the relaxation therefore failed to ease public suffering.
Rahul Chakma, organising secretary of the Sajek Resort-Cottage Owners Association, said the tourism-dependent economy had been hit hardest.
With no tourists visiting the area, resorts, cottages, restaurants, transport services, local shops and other tourism-related businesses have become virtually inactive. The blockade has caused estimated financial losses of Tk30-35 crore so far, he said, warning that the losses could rise further if the disruption continues.
Sajek has more than 116 resorts, 14 restaurants and over 100 small and large shops, Rahul said. With tourists staying away for an extended period, business owners, cottage operators and employees are facing severe hardship and losing their investments.
The blockade has also disrupted road links between Sajek, Baghaichari Upazila Headquarters and Khagrachhari. As a result, residents are struggling to obtain essential food items such as rice and lentils and face uncertainty when travelling for emergencies.
Anitya Tripura, a member of Ward 2 of Sajek Union Parishad, said residents had nearly exhausted their household stocks of food and essential goods. Five shops in Ruilui Para had also run out of essential items, he said, warning that the situation could become more serious if the blockade continued.
Jaupeithang Tripura, headman of Shialdai Mouza and a union parishad member, said local jhum farmers and small traders were unable to take their produce to market because tourists were absent and roads remained blocked. This had brought the rural economy to a virtual standstill, while shortages of medicines and other essential goods were also emerging.
Officer-in-Charge of Sajek police station Tofozzal Hossain said large vehicles were not operating on the roads because of the blockade. Only a few auto-rickshaws and motorcycles were moving occasionally. The situation remained calm, and no major untoward incident had been reported so far, he added.
Protesters have reiterated that they will continue the movement until their demands are met.
The latest blockade began on October 22, following calls by the Sajek Gono Odhikar Rakkha Committee and Sajek Karbari Association. It is the third round of blockades called by the two organisations. Citing security concerns, the Rangamati Zila Parishad temporarily closed the Sajek tourist destination, prompting visitors to leave the area.
Tourism activities had first come to a halt after a continuous blockade beginning on October 11. The programme was relaxed from October 16 to 21 for Durga Puja, but vehicle movement was suspended again from October 22. Repeated blockades and temporary relaxations have failed to produce a permanent resolution.
Sajek Union Parishad Chairman Atulal Chakma said that the administration was working to resolve the crisis, but no satisfactory solution had yet been reached.
Khagrachhari Transport Owners Association president Ayus Chakma said the association had 250 registered vehicles, while the Jeep Owners Association had more than 500. In addition, over 1,500 vehicles, including Mahindra vehicles, Chander Gari, and CNG-run auto-rickshaws, operated in Sajek.
The blockade has cut off the income of drivers and their assistants, while owners who bought vehicles with loans are struggling to pay instalments. The transport sector is suffering estimated daily losses of Tk30-40 lakh across the district, he said.

item.title: Police vehicle set on fire as clashes leave at least 50 injured in Savar
item.description:
At least 50 people, including police personnel, garment workers and passersby, were injured in clashes between workers and police in Savar on Wednesday morning over demands for a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000.
The clashes broke out in the Padma Mor area of Hemayetpur around 8:15am and later spread to Ulail, where confrontations took place in front of the Al-Muslim Group factory around 9am.
During the violence, workers threw bricks and stones at police, who responded with tear gas shells, sound grenades and rubber bullets. A police vehicle belonging to the officer-in-charge of Savar Model Police Station was also set on fire.
The injured included OC Saiful Alam, who sustained serious injuries, according to Dhaka District Superintendent of Police Shamima Parveen. The injured received initial medical treatment.
According to police and local sources, workers gathered near Padma Mor in the morning to press for their wage demands. Tensions escalated when police attempted to clear the road after workers occupied it.
The workers later split into several groups and took positions at different locations, including Padma Mor and Hemayetpur bus stand.
Around 9:10am, protesters blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway, halting traffic in both directions and causing severe congestion.
Industrial Police said workers threw bricks and stones at law enforcement personnel, prompting police to fire tear gas shells to bring the situation under control. A tense atmosphere prevailed in and around Padma Mor.
In Ulail, police also fired tear gas shells and rubber bullets after workers blocked the road and threw bricks and stones during a confrontation.
Shamima Parveen said between 30,000 and 40,000 workers had gathered from both directions in the Padma Mor area in the morning and attacked police. Law enforcement personnel took measures to resist the assault, she said, adding that the protesters set fire to the vehicle belonging to the Savar Model police station OC.
Separately, several garment factories in Hemayetpur, Ulail and nearby areas declared a general holiday amid the unrest. Some workers later returned home peacefully.
Three platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel were deployed in Savar and Ashulia to strengthen security in the industrial zone.
Savar Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) said around 9:30am that workers had occupied the road and the administration was taking steps to restore normal traffic movement.
Lieutenant Colonel Taimun, commander of the BGB Dhaka Battalion deployed in the area, said around three platoons had been stationed at different locations in Savar and Ashulia.
He said BGB personnel were working to disperse people involved in creating disorder and causing public hardship. He also claimed that many of those involved were not actual workers, but people creating unrest.

item.title: Djokovic battles through Paris Masters opener
item.description:
Novak Djokovic battled from behind to beat Valentin Vacherot 6-7 (5/7), 7-5, 6-1 in the first round of the Paris Masters on Tuesday, while Ben Shelton opened his campaign with a comfortable win.
For the Serbian 24-time Grand Slam champion, it marked a return to winning ways at ATP 1000-level tournaments for the first time since his run to the fourth round at Indian Wells back in March.
Djokovic also exacted his own bit of revenge on Vacherot in just the second meeting between the pair -- the Monegasque downed the 39-year-old on his way to a sensational Shanghai Masters title last season.
"I knew that coming into the court it was going to be a very tight match as it was," Djokovic told reporters.
"He's very confident and he's one of the best servers we have in the game," he added of Vacherot, who lifted the second title of his career last week in Basel.
Victory also kept alive Djokovic's chances of landing a spot in the season-ending ATP Finals later in November.
Djokovic is currently 11th in the race to the eight-man tournament in Turin.
However, he insisted his main focus was not the ATP Finals but "to win every match" on his return to the Paris Masters.
In his last appearance at the tournament in 2023, he lifted the trophy for the seventh time.
In an even opening frame, Vacherot got his nose in front at the end of an error-strewn first-set tie-break as he put together a run of four points to take the lead.
After going down a break early in the second set, Djokovic called for a medical timeout for a massage on his right shoulder.
The short stoppage seemed to break Vacherot's concentration as he dropped his serve straight away.
On Djokovic's second break point, the 27-year-old completely misjudged a routine return from his opponent and could only watch in disbelief as the ball bounced on the line right in front of him.
Vacherot then received treatment for a foot issue and soon found himself level at one set each as Djokovic displayed his trademark killer instinct to seize his first break opportunity in the 12th game of the set and send the match to a decider.
The 10th seed ground down Vacherot in his first service game to get his nose in front before then running away with the match.
He will next meet Rinky Hijikata in the second round on Wednesday.
US Open finalist Shelton, who as third seed enjoyed a bye through the first round, put on a commanding display in the night session with a 6-3, 6-4 win over Cameron Norrie.
The world number four needed just 71 minutes to see off the former eighth-ranked Briton, with the only hiccup being a break of his own serve near the end of the second set which the 24-year-old instantly righted to close in on victory.
The American then ceded centre stage to Gael Monfils for a ceremony to honour the career of the hugely popular French player, who retired last month at the age of 40.
Rising star Rafael Jodar was last on centre court but fell in straight sets to former world number two Casper Ruud.
The 20-year-old Spaniard currently sits ninth in the race to Turin, and his defeat meant Italy's Flavio Cobolli secured his spot in the season-ender despite having to withdraw from the Paris Masters with a leg injury.
Elsewhere, Holger Rune, who beat Djokovic in the 2022 final, exited at the first hurdle this time as he continues his return from a lengthy lay-off. The Dane lost 7-5, 6-4 to Tommy Paul.
Matteo Berrettini edged out 14th seed Brandon Nakashima 6-4, 3-6, 7-6 (10/8) and Taylor Fritz showed grit to see off Benjamin Bonzi in three sets.
New home favourite Moise Kouame was unable to recreate his Roland Garros heroics as the French 17-year-old went down 6-3, 6-1 to lucky loser Nuno Borges.
Play continues on Wednesday when world number one Alexander Zverev and seven-time major winner Carlos Alcaraz will both get their tournaments underway at the round-of-32 stage.

item.title: Raphinha, Yamal power Barca to Champions League win over Villa
item.description:
Raphinha struck twice to propel Barcelona to a 3-0 Champions League win over visitors Aston Villa on Tuesday, ending the English side's perfect start to the competition.
Five-time winners Barcelona took an early lead through Lamine Yamal before Raphinha continued his fine goalscoring form with a second-half brace.
Barca bounced back after defeat by champions Paris Saint-Germain in their previous European outing to stay in the hunt for a top eight league phase berth.
Unai Emery's Villa competed well in the first half but were eventually undone by Barca's greater ability in the final third.
The Champions League anthem was not played before the game, as a mark of respect for Tenerife striker Jesus De Miguel, who died on Tuesday morning after an on-pitch collision in a Spanish second division match the previous day, provoking shock across the football world.
"Yes it was (a good win), I want to dedicate this win to the fans, but today I don't want to talk about football, I want to send a message to the family of Jesus -- may he rest in peace," Raphinha told Movistar.
"This can happen to anyone, it's very tough... you're going to play a game and the same thing can happen to you...
"From the club, I want to send a message of strength to the family."
Villa captain John McGinn had only visited the Camp Nou once previously, on a summer holiday as an eight-year-old, and might have expected better weather than the downpour both teams were subjected to.
The skipper might also have expected a more focused start, with Villa handing Barcelona the lead in the seventh minute.
The Spanish champions pressed Aston Villa extremely high and Joao Gomes played a poor pass straight to Yamal in his own box. The 19-year-old winger gladly took the gift and stroked past Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.
"Tonight was a huge learning curve for us and I am sure it will stand us in good stead for the future," McGinn told TNT Sports.
"Barcelona made the right decisions at the right times and scored really good goals."
Yamal's goal was his 14th in the competition across his career, beating Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe's previous record tally of 13 netted as a teenager in the Champions League.
Emery, who endured one of the worst nights of his career away at Barca when helming PSG in 2017 during a 6-1 defeat, may have feared the worst.
However Villa reacted strongly and Matty Cash had a vicious drive deflected narrowly wide before Joao Cancelo blocked Gomes's effort.
Suzuki saved from Anthony Gordon as Villa again struggled to bring the ball out from the back under Barca's pressing.
Garcia was called into action again by Johan Manzambi as the match lurched from end-to-end.
Barcelona extended their lead early in the second half when Fermin Lopez fed Raphinha, who showed quick footwork before finding the bottom corner.
Cancelo set up Raphinha for Barcelona's third with a superb cross with the outside of his boot. The Brazil winger, who has made the number nine position his own this season, pounced from close range for his 19th goal across all competitions.
Yamal sent a shot skidding wide as Barcelona probed for a fourth. It did not come, but the Catalan giants were able to record a first Champions League clean sheet in 19 games.
Flick was pleased with Barcelona keeping Villa at bay.
"It was important that we defended together very compactly," said the German coach.
"The back line played on an amazing level, they defended everything."
Aston Villa are well positioned, provisionally third in the league phase table.
Emery said the match was a good lesson for his side against one of the biggest teams in Europe.
"We must be ruthless in the attacking third, we must be more demanding of ourselves, creating those chances to score," Emery told reporters.
"The 3-0 is maybe more (heavy) than we deserved, but we accept this defeat, taking a lot of information for our improvement."

item.title: United ease troubles with sensational Roma comeback, PSG rampant in Champions League
item.description:
Manchester United fought back from two goals down to beat Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday to hand beleaguered manager Michael Carrick a reprieve, while holders Paris Saint-Germain continued their perfect start in the competition by hitting Villarreal for six.
Looking set for another abject defeat when two behind within 18 minutes through a smart Mathias Soule finish and Donyell Malen's penalty, United staged a thrilling comeback in the second half to turn a poisonous atmosphere at Old Trafford to one of joy.
Matheus Cunha, who was sent off in stoppage time, saved the day for United with a brace in three minutes with the final whistle nearing, sparking wild celebrations in the stands.
Those scenes at the end of the game couldn't have been more different to the anger which pulsated around the ground in the first half, when United fans threw tennis balls and other objects onto the Old Trafford pitch and directed foul-mouthed chants at the club's majority owners, the Glazer family.
"We knew that the fans would be behind us until the last day, we just had to get a result for them," United captain Bruno Fernandes told TNT.
United head into Sunday's match with Aston Villa, beaten 3-0 at Barcelona, in an entirely different mood after punishing slapdash Roma who vanished in the second half after having shown why they look like league title contenders in Italy.
"I spoke at half-time about being positive. Anything can happen here, I've seen it many times over the years," said Carrick.
"You just need something to go our way and the boys were fantastic second half."
Roma, who also threw away a commanding lead against Real Madrid in their only other defeat of the season, failed to deal a knockout blow and crumbled once Bruno Fernandes pulled United back into the game in the 58th minute at the second time of asking from the penalty spot.
The Portuguese thumped home past Roma's third-choice goalkeeper Devis Vasquez, who saved the first attempt but was let down by his teammates encroaching in the penalty area.
And that set up Cunha to hit Roma with a one-two that decided a thrilling encounter and gave Carrick some breathing room with the international break coming up after the weekend.
PSG were in ruthless mood even without star player Khvicha Kvaratskhelia as they beat Villarreal 6-0 on a night in which Europe's elite clubs paid tribute to tragic Tenerife player Jesus de Miguel with a moment's silence before kick-offs.
De Miguel died aged 30 from injuries he suffered in a sickening collision with FC Andorra's goalkeeper in a Spanish second-division match, leaving football in mourning and condolences pouring in from around the globe.
PSG tore into sorry Villarreal, with Joao Neves, Desire Doue, Senny Mayulu and Fabian Ruiz all striking in eight first-half minutes as the French outfit set a record for the fastest four goals scored in a match in Europe's elite club competition.
It certainly didn't look like PSG were missing Kvaratskhelia, Ousmane Dembele, captain Marquinhos and Nuno Mendes, and further strikes from Spain World Cup star Ruiz and teenager David Boly rounded off a stellar performance which put Luis Enrique's team top of the table.
"We were impressive throughout and we are really pleased even if it is very difficult for Villarreal," said Luis Enrique.
"But it is hard when you play against a team like us that presses constantly."
Another team missing a host of stars in Bayern Munich saw off Atletico Madrid 2-0 to move into the top eight positions.
Teenage Germany forward Lennart Karl and Konrad Laimer netted in the second half in Madrid as Bayern triumphed despite the absence of Jamal Musiala, Luis Diaz, Serge Gnabry and Ismael Saibari.
Inter Milan recovered from derby defeat at the weekend with a comfortable 3-0 win over Feyenoord which came through goals from Yann Bisseck, Pio Esposito and Piotr Zielinski.

item.title: Modernizing the airport requires operational competence
item.description:
The launching of e-immigration gates at the arrival counters of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport is a positive step towards digitizing airport services. It goes without saying that the ability for returning citizens to clear border control in under 20 seconds is a long-overdue convenience.
However, celebrating arrival-side automation while departure e-gates sit completely idle exposes a chronic issue in our public sector management: Acquiring expensive, modern hardware without building the underlying digital ecosystem, software integration, or operational capacity required to make it functional.
There is no use for digital services if core operations remain stalled. This is nothing if not a waste of public resources. When digital infrastructure fails to eliminate manual bottlenecks, it becomes a cosmetic facade rather than a genuine upgrade.
This disconnect, much like most of our governance woes, stems from administrative inertia and fragmented planning. Procuring high-tech equipment without ensuring basic software interoperability and staff training is a systemic failure that has plagued most of our public projects for decades.
Passengers traveling through our national airport, much like all citizens receiving public services, deserve to have a smooth and dignified experience. What we don’t need more of are bureaucratic excuses for why multi-million-taka projects don’t deliver what they were meant to.
Modernization for any nation cannot be measured by hardware installations that sit gathering dust. When it comes to having a better international airport, the government must demand accountability, eliminate manual redundancies, and deliver a fully functional, seamless system fit for a modern nation.

item.title: Recognizing our reality
item.description:
While state statistics do suggest a modest 6% growth driven by exports rising for our apparel sector, we must listen to key industry voices marking the reality behind these figures which state that export numbers are misleading.
When factored against soaring production expenses, Bangladesh’s primary export engine could actually be experiencing net negative growth, and this reality cannot be swept under the rug.
To be sure, there is a genuine bright spot: Remittance inflows. Overseas workers sent home $11.465 billion during the July-October period, representing a robust 13% year-on-year surge. This steady inflow from our expatriate workforce once again has offered vital support to our macro-stability.
However, while we can never be thankful enough for the work our expat workers do for the economy, relying on remittances to prop up an economy is an unsustainable strategy, and we need better solutions.
Above all, we must stop taking comfort in superficial statistical milestones and acknowledge our reality, that the economy remains grim: Overall GDP growth has stalled, private sector credit growth languishes at historic lows, and millions of workers remain trapped in a relentless real-wage crisis.
This is the time for our government to work towards genuine national recovery. From restoring liquidity and credit flow to private enterprises to taming persistent inflationary pressures and rebuilding investor confidence, we remain far from solving these issues, and yet they are what must be solved.
Cautious optimism may be warranted, but complacency is fatal. Sustaining export growth is important and necessary, but more important is recognizing where we stand. We must move past short-term statistical relief and focus relentlessly on comprehensive, structural economic revival.

item.title: Garment workers block Dhaka-Aricha highway over wage demands
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Aricha highway in Savar on Wednesday morning, demanding an increase in the minimum wage, an end to the blacklisting of workers and the reversal of what they described as unjust layoffs.
The blockade caused severe traffic congestion, stretching nearly 2km along the highway and leaving thousands of commuters stranded.
Workers from several garment factories gathered near Hemayetpur bus stand around 9am and occupied the highway, bringing traffic to a halt.
As of 9:50am, when this report was filed, the workers were still occupying the road and continuing their protest.
The workers said the rising cost of living had made it increasingly difficult to support their families on the current monthly minimum wage of Tk12,500. They are demanding that the minimum wage be raised to Tk30,000, alongside an end to the blacklisting of workers and arbitrary layoffs.
According to police, workers from several garment factories in the Padma Mor area of Tetuljhora union gathered on Wednesday morning to stage the protest. Workers from AKH Garment Factory, who had initially reported for their shifts, later left the workplace and joined the blockade.
Md Asaduzzaman Noor, officer-in-charge of Savar Highway Police Station, confirmed the blockade and said additional police personnel had been deployed to prevent any untoward incidents.
